The remedy is already known in one dimension from chapter 7: the quadratic bar element has three nodes, and the map between the reference interval \([-1, 1]\) and the actual element (equation (7.28)) uses the same variable \(\xi\) as the shape functions. In the plane we do the same with two coordinates: a reference square is mapped onto a quadrilateral by the same functions with which we interpolate the displacements. Such an element is called isoparametric.

With the triangle the shape functions were already functions of the point \((x, y)\), so nothing had to be mapped. With an isoparametric element three questions arise. When is the map good, that is one to one and with a Jacobian determinant that is nowhere zero or negative, so that we may use theorem 4.59? How do we get the strain if we know the shape functions as functions of the coordinates \(\xi\) and \(\eta\), not of \(x\) and \(y\)? And does the field of the element stay continuous across shared sides, as the Ritz theorems of section 15.2 require, and does it contain the linear fields that the patch test of section 15.7 requires? The idealizations are as before: the material is linear elastic, the strains are small and the material is isotropic (steel, \(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\)), but this section computes only geometry and shape functions, the material enters in the following ones.

15.5.1 The square and four shape functions

The reference element is the square \(K = [-1, 1]^2\) in the plane with natural coordinates (naravni koordinati) \(\xi\) and \(\eta\). Its four nodes are numbered counterclockwise from the lower left: \(1 = (-1, -1)\), \(2 = (1, -1)\), \(3 = (1, 1)\), \(4 = (-1, 1)\), and we write the coordinates of node \(i\) as \((\xi_{\mathrm{i}}, \eta_{\mathrm{i}})\).

We draw the square with side \(2\), so that its sides are always \(\xi = \pm 1\) and \(\eta = \pm 1\), whatever the shape of the actual element. Each node has one function that equals \(1\) in it and \(0\) in the other nodes. For node \(1\) this is a product of two linear functions, equal to \(1\) at \(\xi = \eta = -1\) and zero on the sides \(\xi = 1\) and \(\eta = 1\). The level lines of this function are hyperbolas, since the product \((1 - \xi)(1 - \eta)\) at a constant value is a hyperbola, and the value falls from \(1\) at node \(1\) to \(0\) on both opposite sides. In general, for node \(i\) the following definition holds.

Definition 15.28 Shape functions of the four-node element (oblikovne funkcije štirikotnika)

The shape functions of the element with four nodes on the square \(K\), called Q4 (quadrilateral, four nodes), are

\[N_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi, \eta) = \tfrac14\,(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\xi)\,(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\,\eta) , \qquad i = 1, 2, 3, 4 . \tag{15.22}\]

Source: COOK, section 6.2, PDF p. 220: shape functions of equation (6.2-3), each equal to \(1\) in its own node and \(0\) in the others. ONATE1, chapter 6, PDF p. 211. The name Q4 is used the same way there and in COOK.

Lemma 15.29 Properties of the four-node shape functions (lastnosti oblikovnih funkcij štirikotnika)

For the functions (15.22):

  1. \(N_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi_{\mathrm{j}}, \eta_{\mathrm{j}}) = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for \(i, j = 1, \dots, 4\).
  2. \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,N_{\mathrm{i}} = \xi\) and \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\,N_{\mathrm{i}} = \eta\).
  3. On the side \(\eta = -1\), \(N_3 = N_4 = 0\) and \(N_1 = (1 - \xi)/2\), \(N_2 = (1 + \xi)/2\). The same holds for the other three sides: on each side only the functions of its two nodes are different from zero, and both are linear along the side.
  4. \(N_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\) everywhere on \(K\).
Proof

We must show four claims. The first by substitution, the second by splitting the sum over the nodes into a product of two sums, the third and fourth by writing the functions out.

  1. Let \(i \ne j\). Then \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}} \ne \xi_{\mathrm{j}}\) or \(\eta_{\mathrm{i}} \ne \eta_{\mathrm{j}}\), and each coordinate is \(\pm 1\), so \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}} = -1\) or \(\eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}} = -1\) and one factor \(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}}\) or \(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}}\) is zero. For \(i = j\) each factor is \(1 + 1 = 2\) and \(N_{\mathrm{i}} = \tfrac14 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 1\).
  2. The four nodes have all four combinations \((\xi_{\mathrm{i}}, \eta_{\mathrm{i}}) \in \{\pm 1\}^2\), each exactly once. Hence \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} = \tfrac14 \big(\sum_{\mathrm{a} = \pm 1}(1 + a\xi)\big)\big(\sum_{\mathrm{b} = \pm 1}(1 + b\eta)\big) = \tfrac14 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 1\).
  3. Similarly \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,N_{\mathrm{i}} = \tfrac14 \big(\sum_{\mathrm{a} = \pm 1} a\,(1 + a\xi)\big)\big(\sum_{\mathrm{b} = \pm 1}(1 + b\eta)\big) = \tfrac14 \cdot 2\xi \cdot 2 = \xi\), because \((1 + \xi) - (1 - \xi) = 2\xi\). For \(\eta\) the computation is the same.
  4. At \(\eta = -1\) every function with \(\eta_{\mathrm{i}} = +1\) has the factor \(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta = 0\), these are \(N_3\) and \(N_4\). The remaining two have the factor \(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta = 2\), so \(N_1 = \tfrac14 (1 - \xi) \cdot 2 = (1 - \xi)/2\) and \(N_2 = (1 + \xi)/2\). The sides \(\xi = 1\), \(\eta = 1\), \(\xi = -1\) are the same after exchanging the roles.
  5. On \(K\), \(|\xi| \le 1\) and \(|\eta| \le 1\), so both factors \(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi \ge 0\) and \(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta \ge 0\), and the product is not negative.

Source: COOK, section 6.2, PDF p. 220: the check that each function is \(1\) in its own node and \(0\) in the others. Points 2 to 4 and the proof are ours.

15.5.2 The same functions for position and for field

Now we say what isoparametric means. The element has nodes at positions \(\vek p_{\mathrm{i}} = (x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{i}})\) and displacements \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = (u_{\mathrm{i}}, v_{\mathrm{i}})\). We use the functions \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) twice, once for the position of a point of the element, once for its displacement.

Definition 15.30 Isoparametric element (izoparametrični element)

Let \(K\) be the reference region, in the plane the square \([-1, 1]^2\), in space the cube \([-1, 1]^3\) (section 15.10), and let \(N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}}\) be shape functions with \(N_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek\xi_{\mathrm{j}}) = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) in the nodes \(\vek\xi_{\mathrm{j}}\) of \(K\) and \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\). The isoparametric element with nodes \(\vek p_1, \dots, \vek p_{\mathrm{m}}\) is the set of points \(\Phi(K)\) with the geometric map

\[\Phi(\xi, \eta) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{m} N_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi, \eta)\,\vek p_{\mathrm{i}} , \tag{15.23}\]

with the displacement field that has the value

\[\vek u_{\mathrm{h}}\big(\Phi(\xi, \eta)\big) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{m} N_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi, \eta)\,\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} \tag{15.24}\]

at the point \(\Phi(\xi, \eta)\), where \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}}\) are the nodal displacements. For \(m = 4\) and the functions of definition 15.28 this is the quadrilateral Q4.

Source: COOK, section 6.2, PDF p. 220: the same shape functions interpolate coordinates and displacements of a point of the element from the values at the nodes. COOK, section 6.1, PDF p. 217: an element in which the number of nodes for the position equals the number for the field is isoparametric, otherwise subparametric or superparametric.

History tells why this recipe arose and how it got its name. The isoparametric formulation began with four-node plane elements introduced by Taig in 1958, and publication outside company reports began with Irons in 1966. Irons developed elements with curved sides and is credited with the name "isoparametric" (COOK, PDF p. 217, ONATE1, PDF p. 212). The reason for curved sides is the same as ours: with triangles with straight sides a curved boundary is replaced by a polygonal line, while with an element with a curved side the boundary can follow the shape of the body.

Let us see on a concrete quadrilateral what the map does. Let the nodes be (in mm) \(\vek p_1 = (0, 0)\), \(\vek p_2 = (40, 0)\), \(\vek p_3 = (36, 30)\) and \(\vek p_4 = (4, 24)\), the area of this image will be \(972\) mm². By equation (15.22) the point \((\xi, \eta) = (\tfrac12, -\tfrac12)\) has the values \(N_1, \dots, N_4\) equal to \(0{,}1875\), \(0{,}5625\), \(0{,}1875\) and \(0{,}0625\), with sum \(1\) (lemma 15.29, point 2), and goes to \(x = 0{,}5625 \cdot 40 + 0{,}1875 \cdot 36 + 0{,}0625 \cdot 4 = 29{,}5\) mm and \(y = 0{,}1875 \cdot 30 + 0{,}0625 \cdot 24 = 7{,}125\) mm (num-05.out, part D). The centre \((0, 0)\) goes to \((20; 13{,}5)\) mm, which is not the centroid of the quadrilateral, since that lies at \((20{,}74; 13{,}06)\) mm.

First the square on the left with four numbered nodes, the axes \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) and six lines, blue at constant \(\xi\) and orange at constant \(\eta\). The arrow \(\Phi\) carries it to the right into the quadrilateral with the same node labels. The lines of the square went over into segments, which are no longer perpendicular and no longer equally spaced. Why segments, the next lemma says. The centre of the square fell on \((20; 13{,}5)\) mm, and the numbers at the corners and at the centre are values of the Jacobian determinant, which we define right away.

The matrix of partial derivatives of the map, \(\mat F = \begin{bmatrix} x_\xi & x_\eta \\ y_\xi & y_\eta \end{bmatrix}\) (a subscript means a derivative, this is the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\) of chapter 4), and its determinant \(J = \det\mat F\) are called the Jacobian matrix and the Jacobian determinant (Jacobijeva matrika in Jacobijeva determinanta). For the bar this was the factor \(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}\xi = h/2\) of equation (7.28), in the plane it is a \(2 \times 2\) determinant. For the cross product of two plane vectors we write \(\vek u \times \vek v = u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}} - u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}}\), so \(J = \Phi_\xi \times \Phi_\eta\).

Lemma 15.31 Map and Jacobian determinant of the four-node element (preslikava in Jacobijeva determinanta štirikotnika)

Let \(\Phi\) be the map (15.23) of a quadrilateral Q4 with nodes \(\vek p_1, \dots, \vek p_4\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek p_{\mathrm{i}+1} - \vek p_{\mathrm{i}}\) the side vectors (indices cyclic, \(\vek p_5 = \vek p_1\)). Let

\[\vek a = \tfrac14(\vek p_1 + \vek p_2 + \vek p_3 + \vek p_4) , \quad \vek b = \tfrac14(-\vek p_1 + \vek p_2 + \vek p_3 - \vek p_4) , \quad \vek c = \tfrac14(-\vek p_1 - \vek p_2 + \vek p_3 + \vek p_4) , \quad \vek d = \tfrac14(\vek p_1 - \vek p_2 + \vek p_3 - \vek p_4) .\]

Then:

  1. \(\Phi(\xi, \eta) = \vek a + \vek b\,\xi + \vek c\,\eta + \vek d\,\xi\eta\). At constant \(\eta\) the function \(\xi \mapsto \Phi(\xi, \eta)\) is affine, at constant \(\xi\) the function \(\eta \mapsto \Phi(\xi, \eta)\) is affine. The sides of the square go over into the segments \(\vek p_1\vek p_2\), \(\vek p_2\vek p_3\), \(\vek p_3\vek p_4\), \(\vek p_4\vek p_1\).
  2. \(J(\xi, \eta) = \vek b\times\vek c + (\vek b\times\vek d)\,\xi + (\vek d\times\vek c)\,\eta\), so \(J\) is an affine function of \(\xi\) and \(\eta\).
  3. The value at corner \(i\) is \(J_{\mathrm{i}} = \tfrac14\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), and \(J(0, 0) = \tfrac14 (J_1 + J_2 + J_3 + J_4)\).
Proof

We must show three points. The first by collecting terms, the second by differentiating, the third by computing at the four corners.

  1. In equation (15.23) we insert \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) from equation (15.22) and collect the terms in \(1\), \(\xi\), \(\eta\) and \(\xi\eta\). The coefficient of \(1\) is \(\tfrac14\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \vek p_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek a\), of \(\xi\) it is \(\tfrac14\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\vek p_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek b\), of \(\eta\) it is \(\tfrac14\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\vek p_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek c\) and of \(\xi\eta\) it is \(\tfrac14\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{i}}\vek p_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek d\), because \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{i}} = 1, -1, 1, -1\).
  2. At constant \(\eta\), \(\Phi = (\vek a + \vek c\eta) + (\vek b + \vek d\eta)\,\xi\), an affine function of \(\xi\), and the same at constant \(\xi\). At \(\eta = -1\) this is a segment that by lemma 15.29, point 1, has the values \(\vek p_1\) and \(\vek p_2\) at \(\xi = \mp 1\). The other three sides are the same.
  3. The derivatives are \(\Phi_\xi = \vek b + \vek d\eta\) and \(\Phi_\eta = \vek c + \vek d\xi\), so \(J = (\vek b + \vek d\eta)\times(\vek c + \vek d\xi) = \vek b\times\vek c + \xi\,\vek b\times\vek d + \eta\,\vek d\times\vek c + \xi\eta\,\vek d\times\vek d\), and \(\vek d\times\vek d = 0\).
  4. Corners. The computations of step 1 give \(\vek b - \vek d = \tfrac12\vek e_1\), \(\vek b + \vek d = -\tfrac12\vek e_3\), \(\vek c - \vek d = -\tfrac12\vek e_4\) and \(\vek c + \vek d = \tfrac12\vek e_2\). At \((-1, -1)\) we have \(\Phi_\xi = \vek b - \vek d\) and \(\Phi_\eta = \vek c - \vek d\), so \(J_1 = \tfrac12\vek e_1\times(-\tfrac12\vek e_4) = \tfrac14\vek e_4\times\vek e_1\). At \((1, -1)\), \(J_2 = \tfrac12\vek e_1\times\tfrac12\vek e_2\), at \((1, 1)\), \(J_3 = (-\tfrac12\vek e_3)\times\tfrac12\vek e_2 = \tfrac14\vek e_2\times\vek e_3\), and at \((-1, 1)\), \(J_4 = (-\tfrac12\vek e_3)\times(-\tfrac12\vek e_4) = \tfrac14\vek e_3\times\vek e_4\).
  5. For an affine function \(J = j_0 + j_1\xi + j_2\eta\) we have \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} J_{\mathrm{i}} = 4 j_0 + j_1\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{i}} + j_2\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{i}} = 4j_0 = 4J(0, 0)\), because \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\).

Source: COOK, section 6.2, PDF p. 221: \(J\) is the determinant of the Jacobian matrix, for a rectangle and a parallelogram it is constant, \(J = A/4\). The proof, the affinity of \(J\) and the values at the corners are ours.

For our quadrilateral \(\vek a = (20; 13{,}5)\) mm, \(\vek b = (18; 1{,}5)\) mm, \(\vek c = (0; 13{,}5)\) mm and \(\vek d = (-2; 1{,}5)\) mm, so \(\vek b\times\vek c = 243\), \(\vek b\times\vek d = 30\) and \(\vek d\times\vek c = -27\) mm². Hence \(J = 243 + 30\,\xi - 27\,\eta\) mm², at the corners \(240\), \(300\), \(246\) and \(186\) mm² and at the centre \(243\) mm², as figure 15.20 shows (num-05.out, part B). The mean of the four corner values is indeed \(243\). For a \(40 \times 30\) mm rectangle \(J = 300\) mm² everywhere, one quarter of the area \(1200\) mm², in agreement with the statement in COOK.

15.5.3 When a quadrilateral is a curved box

Theorem 4.59 requires the map to be injective on an open set around \(K\) and to have a nonzero Jacobian determinant, and definition 4.65 further requires it to be positive. For a quadrilateral this is simple, because \(J\) is an affine function.

Theorem 15.32 A quadrilateral with positive determinant at the corners is a curved box (štirikotnik s pozitivno determinanto v ogliščih je ukrivljen kvader)

Let \(\Phi\) be the map of a quadrilateral Q4 and let \(J_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) at all four corners (\(i = 1, \dots, 4\), lemma 15.31). Then:

  1. \(J > 0\) on the closed square \(K\) and on the open square \(K_\varepsilon = (-1 - \varepsilon, 1 + \varepsilon)^2\) for \(\varepsilon > 0\) small enough.
  2. The map \(\Phi\) is injective on \(K_\varepsilon\).
  3. The map \(\Phi\) satisfies conditions 1 to 3 of definition 4.65, written for the plane. The set \(Q = \Phi(K)\) is therefore a curved box in the plane, and for every continuous function \(f\) on \(Q\)
    \[\int_{\mathrm{Q}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{K}} f\big(\Phi(\xi, \eta)\big)\,J(\xi, \eta)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{15.25}\]
  4. The area of the quadrilateral is \(A = 4J(0, 0) = J_1 + J_2 + J_3 + J_4\).
Proof

We must show four claims. The positivity of \(J\) follows from \(J\) being a weighted sum of the corner values with nonnegative weights. Injectivity follows from the difference of the images of two points being the Jacobian matrix at the midpoint times the difference of the points. Then we apply the change of variables theorem.

  1. The function \(J\) is affine (lemma 15.31, point 2), so by lemma 15.29, point 2, \(J = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} J_{\mathrm{i}}\,N_{\mathrm{i}}\). For affine \(J = j_0 + j_1\xi + j_2\eta\) the sum has the value \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} J_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} = j_0\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} + j_1\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} + j_2\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}\), which is \(j_0 + j_1\xi + j_2\eta\).
  2. By point 4 of lemma 15.29 the \(N_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\) and their sum is \(1\), so \(J \ge \min_{\mathrm{i}} J_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) on \(K\).
  3. Values on the open square. An affine function \(j_0 + j_1\xi + j_2\eta\) reaches its smallest value on a square at one of the corners, because each of the terms \(j_1\xi\) and \(j_2\eta\) reaches its smallest value at an end of its interval. The corners of the square \(K_\varepsilon\) are \((1 + \varepsilon)(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}, \eta_{\mathrm{i}})\) and \(J\big((1 + \varepsilon)(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}, \eta_{\mathrm{i}})\big) = J(0, 0) + (1 + \varepsilon)\,(J_{\mathrm{i}} - J(0, 0)) = J_{\mathrm{i}} + \varepsilon\,(J_{\mathrm{i}} - J(0, 0))\). At \(\varepsilon = 0\) this equals \(J_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) and it is continuous in \(\varepsilon\), so for small enough \(\varepsilon\) it is positive at all four corners and \(J > 0\) on the whole \(K_\varepsilon\).
  4. Let \(P = (\xi_{\mathrm{P}}, \eta_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(Q' = (\xi_{\mathrm{Q}'}, \eta_{\mathrm{Q}'})\) be points of \(K_\varepsilon\) and \(\vek\delta = Q' - P\). By lemma 15.31, point 1, \(\Phi(Q') - \Phi(P) = \vek b\,\delta_\xi + \vek c\,\delta_\eta + \vek d\,(\xi_{\mathrm{Q}'}\eta_{\mathrm{Q}'} - \xi_{\mathrm{P}}\eta_{\mathrm{P}})\). We have \(\xi_{\mathrm{Q}'}\eta_{\mathrm{Q}'} - \xi_{\mathrm{P}}\eta_{\mathrm{P}} = \tfrac12\big[(\xi_{\mathrm{P}} + \xi_{\mathrm{Q}'})(\eta_{\mathrm{Q}'} - \eta_{\mathrm{P}}) + (\xi_{\mathrm{Q}'} - \xi_{\mathrm{P}})(\eta_{\mathrm{P}} + \eta_{\mathrm{Q}'})\big] = \xi_{\mathrm{M}}\,\delta_\eta + \eta_{\mathrm{M}}\,\delta_\xi\) with the midpoint \(M = (\xi_{\mathrm{M}}, \eta_{\mathrm{M}})\) of the segment \(PQ'\). So \(\Phi(Q') - \Phi(P) = (\vek b + \vek d\,\eta_{\mathrm{M}})\,\delta_\xi + (\vek c + \vek d\,\xi_{\mathrm{M}})\,\delta_\eta = \mat F(M)\,\vek\delta\).
  5. The square \(K_\varepsilon\) is convex, so \(M \in K_\varepsilon\) and \(\det\mat F(M) = J(M) > 0\) by step 3. A matrix with nonzero determinant is invertible (lemma 2.51), so for \(\vek\delta \ne \vek 0\) also \(\mat F(M)\,\vek\delta \ne \vek 0\) and \(\Phi(Q') \ne \Phi(P)\). This is point 2.
  6. The components of \(\Phi\) are polynomials, so they have continuous partial derivatives of all orders on the whole plane, \(\Phi\) is injective and \(J > 0\) on \(K_\varepsilon\). These are conditions 1 to 3 of definition 4.65. The square \(K\) is a set with area, so equation (15.25) holds by theorem 4.59 (in the plane), with \(|J| = J\).
  7. Area. For \(f = 1\) equation (15.25) gives \(A = \int_{\mathrm{K}} J\,\mathrm{d}A\). The integral of an affine function over the square is \(4j_0\), since \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \xi\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{K}} \eta\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) by theorem 4.9, and \(4j_0 = 4J(0, 0) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} J_{\mathrm{i}}\) by step 5 of lemma 15.31.

Source: COOK, section 6.2, PDF pp. 221 and 222: \(J\) is the factor that multiplies \(\mathrm{d}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\eta\) into the area element, nodes must be numbered counterclockwise so that \(J\) is not negative. ONATE1, section 6.1, PDF p. 211: the Jacobian determinant must have a constant sign over the element, for the linear quadrilateral this is satisfied if no internal angle is equal to or larger than \(180^\circ\) (the source states the condition without proof). The proof is ours.

The condition \(J_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) has a geometric meaning. By point 3 of lemma 15.31, \(J_{\mathrm{i}} = \tfrac14|\vek e_{\mathrm{i}-1}||\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}|\sin\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\), where \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the angle by which the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) turns counterclockwise into \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), that is the exterior angle at corner \(i\). A positive \(J_{\mathrm{i}}\) means that the boundary turns left at corner \(i\), the interior angle is smaller than \(180^\circ\). The condition of theorem 15.32 therefore means four turns to the left, that is a convex quadrilateral with nodes numbered counterclockwise (ONATE1, PDF p. 211, states the same condition for the interior angles). The example in the map of figure 15.20 has all four \(J_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) and is convex.

What happens if the condition is not met? Take a quadrilateral with nodes \((0, 0)\), \((40, 0)\), \((14, 8)\) and \((4, 24)\) mm, which differs from the previous one only in node \(3\), pulled inward. The polygon with these four vertices is an ordinary, nonconvex quadrilateral, and whoever draws it sees nothing wrong.

Lemma 15.33 A folded quadrilateral (zložen štirikotnik)

Let \(\Phi\) be the map of a quadrilateral Q4 with nodes \((0, 0)\), \((40, 0)\), \((14, 8)\) and \((4, 24)\) mm. Then:

  1. \(J = 78 - 80\,\xi - 82\,\eta\) mm², at the corners \(J_1 = 240\), \(J_2 = 80\), \(J_3 = -84\) and \(J_4 = 76\) mm².
  2. \(J = 0\) on the segment \(80\,\xi + 82\,\eta = 78\) from the point \((-0{,}05; 1)\) to \((1; -1/41)\), \(J < 0\) above it.
  3. The points \(P = (0{,}6; 0{,}6)\) and \(Q = (0{,}36; 15/41)\) of the square have the same image \(\Phi(P) = \Phi(Q) = (16; 8{,}96)\) mm, and \(J(P) = -19{,}2\), \(J(Q) = +19{,}2\) mm². So \(\Phi\) is not injective on \(K\).
  4. The midpoint \(M = (0{,}48; 19{,}8/41)\) of the segment \(PQ\) lies on the segment of point 2, so \(J(M) = 0\) and \(\mat F(M)\) is singular.
Proof

We must show four claims by computation with lemma 15.31 and equation (15.23).

  1. The vectors are \(\vek b = (-0 + 40 + 14 - 4,\ 0 + 0 + 8 - 24)/4 = (12{,}5; -4)\), \(\vek c = (0 - 40 + 14 + 4,\ 0 - 0 + 8 + 24)/4 = (-5{,}5; 8)\) and \(\vek d = (0 - 40 + 14 - 4,\ 0 - 0 + 8 - 24)/4 = (-7{,}5; -4)\). So \(\vek b\times\vek c = 12{,}5\cdot 8 - (-4)(-5{,}5) = 78\), \(\vek b\times\vek d = 12{,}5\cdot(-4) - (-4)(-7{,}5) = -80\) and \(\vek d\times\vek c = (-7{,}5)\cdot 8 - (-4)(-5{,}5) = -82\). The values at the corners follow from \(J_{\mathrm{i}} = \tfrac14\vek e_{\mathrm{i}-1}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) or by inserting \((\pm 1, \pm 1)\) into \(J\). At node \(3\), \(\vek e_2 = (-26, 8)\) and \(\vek e_3 = (-10, 16)\), so \(J_3 = \tfrac14\,(-26\cdot 16 - 8\cdot(-10)) = -84\).
  2. The equation \(J = 0\) is a line. At \(\eta = 1\) it gives \(\xi = -4/80 = -0{,}05\), at \(\xi = 1\) it gives \(\eta = -2/82 = -1/41\). Both points are on the boundary of \(K\). Since \(J\) is affine, it has one sign on one side of the line and the opposite on the other, and it is negative on the side where corner \(3\) lies, with \(J_3 = -84 < 0\).
  3. At \(P = (0{,}6; 0{,}6)\) the \(N_1, \dots, N_4\) are \(0{,}04\), \(0{,}16\), \(0{,}64\), \(0{,}16\) and \(\Phi(P) = (0{,}16\cdot 40 + 0{,}64\cdot 14 + 0{,}16\cdot 4,\ 0{,}64\cdot 8 + 0{,}16\cdot 24) = (16; 8{,}96)\). At \(Q = (0{,}36; 15/41)\) the \(N_{\mathrm{i}} = (4{,}16;\ 8{,}84;\ 19{,}04;\ 8{,}96)/41\) with sum \(1\) and \(\Phi(Q) = \big((8{,}84\cdot 40 + 19{,}04\cdot 14 + 8{,}96\cdot 4)/41,\ (19{,}04\cdot 8 + 8{,}96\cdot 24)/41\big) = (656/41;\ 367{,}36/41) = (16; 8{,}96)\). Further \(J(P) = 78 - 48 - 49{,}2 = -19{,}2\) and \(J(Q) = 78 - 28{,}8 - 30 = 19{,}2\).
  4. By step 4 of the proof of theorem 15.32, \(\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P) = \mat F(M)\,(Q - P)\) for the midpoint \(M\) and \(Q - P \ne \vek 0\). The left side is zero, so \(\mat F(M)\) is singular and \(J(M) = 0\). Directly: \(J(M) = 78 - 80\cdot 0{,}48 - 82\cdot 19{,}8/41 = 78 - 38{,}4 - 39{,}6 = 0\).

Source: COOK, section 6.2, PDF p. 222: if the numbering does not run counterclockwise, \(J\) becomes negative over part or all of the element. COOK, section 6.11, PDF p. 250, figure 6.11-2: in badly distorted elements a Gauss point lies outside the element and \(J\) is negative there, an acceptable element must not have a negative \(J\) at any Gauss point. The example and the computations are ours (num-05.out, parts B and G).

Let us look at the figure. The square with nodes \(1\) to \(4\) is the same as before. The line \(J = 0\) cuts a triangle out of the square at corner \(3\), with corners \((-0{,}05; 1)\), \((1; -1/41)\) and \((1; 1)\), in which \(J < 0\). In the square are the points \(P\) and \(Q\), \(P\) in this triangle and \(Q\) outside it. The arrow \(\Phi\) leads to the quadrilateral on the right, which has node \(3\) pulled inward. The image of the line \(J = 0\) is a curve that runs from \((8{,}75; 16{,}4)\) to \((27{,}3; 3{,}9)\) mm, and the region between it and node \(3\) is the image of the triangle with \(J < 0\). Both \(P\) and \(Q\) have the same image \((16; 8{,}96)\) mm: the map is folded there, like the crease of a sheet of paper. The numbers at the corners are \(J_{\mathrm{i}}\) in mm², the third is negative.

The fault arises already at one corner, although the quadrilateral looks ordinary. The integral \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} J\,\mathrm{d}A\) is \(312\) mm², the area of the polygon, but \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} |J|\,\mathrm{d}A = 342{,}12\) mm² (num-05.out, part B). For a folded map theorem 4.59 does not hold, because it is not injective, and \(\int|J|\) is not the area of the image. At the four points \((\pm 1/\sqrt3, \pm 1/\sqrt3)\), where the \(2 \times 2\) rule of section 15.6 will evaluate the integrand of the element matrix, \(J\) is \(171{,}5\), \(79{,}2\), \(-15{,}5\) and \(76{,}9\) mm², so negative in one of them. That point would contribute to the integral with a negative weight \(J\).

15.5.4 The strain from the inverse of the Jacobian matrix

The displacement field of the element (15.24) is a function of \((\xi, \eta)\), but we need the strains as derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\). For the bar \(\mathrm{d}/\mathrm{d}x = (2/h)\,\mathrm{d}/\mathrm{d}\xi\) was enough, because the ratio is constant. In the plane a matrix appears.

Lemma 15.34 Derivatives of the shape functions with respect to x and y (odvodi oblikovnih funkcij po x in y)

Let an isoparametric element have \(J > 0\) at the point \((\xi, \eta)\) and let \(g(\xi, \eta)\) be a smooth function with \(g = f\circ\Phi\) for some function \(f(x, y)\) on the element. Then

\[\begin{pmatrix} f_{\mathrm{x}} \\ f_{\mathrm{y}} \end{pmatrix} = \mat F^{-\T}\begin{pmatrix} g_\xi \\ g_\eta \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat F^{-1} = \frac{1}{J}\begin{bmatrix} y_\eta & -x_\eta \\ -y_\xi & x_\xi \end{bmatrix} . \tag{15.26}\]

In particular \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x = (y_\eta N_{\mathrm{i},\xi} - y_\xi N_{\mathrm{i},\eta})/J\) and \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y = (-x_\eta N_{\mathrm{i},\xi} + x_\xi N_{\mathrm{i},\eta})/J\), and for the strain \(\vek\varepsilon = (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}, \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}})^\T = \mat B\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (u_1, v_1, \dots, u_4, v_4)^\T\) the matrix \(\mat B\) of size \(3 \times 8\) has in columns \(2i - 1\) and \(2i\) the block

\[\mat B_{\mathrm{i}} = \begin{bmatrix} \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x & 0 \\ 0 & \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y \\ \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y & \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x \end{bmatrix} . \tag{15.27}\]
Proof

We must show the relation between the derivatives, its inverse and the form of the matrix \(\mat B\).

  1. By the chain rule (lemma 4.43), \(g_\xi = f_{\mathrm{x}}\,x_\xi + f_{\mathrm{y}}\,y_\xi\) and \(g_\eta = f_{\mathrm{x}}\,x_\eta + f_{\mathrm{y}}\,y_\eta\), so \((g_\xi, g_\eta)^\T = \mat F^\T\,(f_{\mathrm{x}}, f_{\mathrm{y}})^\T\). The derivatives \(f_{\mathrm{x}}, f_{\mathrm{y}}\) exist, because by theorem 4.51 \(\Phi\) is smoothly invertible (\(J \ne 0\)).
  2. The matrix \(\mat F^\T\) has determinant \(J \ne 0\), so it is invertible, and the inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix is the adjugate matrix divided by the determinant. This gives the equations for \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x\) and \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y\) with \(g = N_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  3. The strains of the field \(\vek u_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek u_{\mathrm{i}}\) are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{h}}/\partial x = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} (\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x)\,u_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} (\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y)\,v_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{h}}/\partial y + \partial v_{\mathrm{h}}/\partial x = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} (\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y\,u_{\mathrm{i}} + \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x\,v_{\mathrm{i}})\). These are the rows of the product \(\mat B\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the blocks \(\mat B_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Source: COOK, section 6.2, PDF pp. 220 to 222: the derivation of the derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) with the Jacobian matrix, equations (6.2-4) to (6.2-11), and the matrix \(\mat B\) as a product of three matrices. The proof is ours.

Let us try it on the quadrilateral with nodes \((0, 0)\), \((40, 0)\), \((36, 30)\), \((4, 24)\) mm. At the centre \(\mat F = \begin{bmatrix} 18 & 0 \\ 1{,}5 & 13{,}5 \end{bmatrix}\) mm and \(J = 243\) mm². The derivatives of \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) with respect to \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) are \((-\tfrac14, -\tfrac14)\) for \(N_1\), \((\tfrac14, -\tfrac14)\) for \(N_2\), \((\tfrac14, \tfrac14)\) for \(N_3\) and \((-\tfrac14, \tfrac14)\) for \(N_4\), and by equation (15.26) \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x = (-0{,}012346;\ 0{,}015432;\ 0{,}012346;\ -0{,}015432)\) and \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y = (-0{,}018519;\ -0{,}018519;\ 0{,}018519;\ 0{,}018519)\) per mm (num-05.out, part D). The first value is \((13{,}5\cdot(-\tfrac14) - 1{,}5\cdot(-\tfrac14))/243 = -3/243\). The denominator \(J\) is in every entry of \(\mat B\). For the triangle \(\mat B\) of equation (15.19) was a constant matrix, here it depends on the point \((\xi, \eta)\) and is a ratio of polynomials, which will matter in section 15.6. On notation: \(\mat B\) is the same matrix as for the triangle (the matrix that gives the strain from the column of nodal displacements), only dependent on the point. The row \(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}\) of chapter 7 is its one-dimensional form. The determinant \(J\) here is the \(J_\Phi\) of chapter 4.

The field \(\vek u_{\mathrm{h}}\) in the element is a polynomial in \(\xi\) and \(\eta\). In the coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) it is a polynomial for all nodal displacements if the map is affine, because then \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) are affine functions of \(x\) and \(y\). For a rectangle \(x = x_{\mathrm{c}} + a\,\xi\), \(y = y_{\mathrm{c}} + b\,\eta\) the field is bilinear in \(x\) and \(y\): it contains \(1\), \(x\), \(y\) and \(xy\), but not \(x^2\) or \(y^2\). For a general quadrilateral we get \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) from \(x\) and \(y\) by solving a quadratic equation, so they contain a square root and the field is in general not a polynomial in \(x\) and \(y\). For our quadrilateral, for example, \(\xi = x/40 + y/30 - 5 + \sqrt{9x^2 + 24xy + 16y^2 + 2880x - 4800y + 230\,400}/120\) (\(x\) and \(y\) in mm, SymPy, it gives \(-1\) at node \(1\) and \(1\) at node \(2\)). Because the field on a rectangle lacks the terms \(x^2\) and \(y^2\), Q4 does not describe bending exactly (section 15.7).

15.5.5 Linear fields and compatibility on shared sides

An isoparametric element must meet two conditions that the Ritz theory of section 15.2 demands. The field must be continuous across a shared side with another element (so that it lies in the space \(X\) of piecewise smooth fields, definition 15.13), and it must contain the linear fields, so that on any mesh the exact solution with constant strain is in the family.

Lemma 15.35 Linear fields belong to the isoparametric family (linearna polja so v družini izoparametričnih elementov)

Let an isoparametric element (definition 15.30) have nodal positions \(\vek p_{\mathrm{i}}\), and let \(\vek a_0 \in \mathbb{R}^2\) be a column and \(\mat G\) a \(2 \times 2\) matrix of constants. If the nodal displacements are \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek a_0 + \mat G\,\vek p_{\mathrm{i}}\), the field of the element at every point of the element is

\[\vek u_{\mathrm{h}}(\vek x) = \vek a_0 + \mat G\,\vek x . \tag{15.28}\]

The strain \(\vek\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat G + \mat G^\T)\) is then constant everywhere on the element and equal to the strain of this linear field.

Proof

We must show equation (15.28) and the strain.

  1. By equation (15.24), at the point \(\vek x = \Phi(\xi, \eta)\) the value is \(\vek u_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\vek a_0 + \mat G\,\vek p_{\mathrm{i}}) = \vek a_0\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} + \mat G\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek p_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  2. By definition \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) and by equation (15.23) \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek p_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek x\). So \(\vek u_{\mathrm{h}}(\vek x) = \vek a_0 + \mat G\,\vek x\).
  3. The derivatives of this field are \(\partial u/\partial x = G_{11}\), \(\partial u/\partial y = G_{12}\), \(\partial v/\partial x = G_{21}\), \(\partial v/\partial y = G_{22}\), which gives the strain \((G_{11}, G_{22}, G_{12} + G_{21})\), where the third component is \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). This is the strain of the linear field, whatever the shape of the element.

Source: COOK, section 6.12, PDF p. 252: an isoparametric element contains a complete linear polynomial, which is necessary for convergence. The same source explains that this fails for a superparametric element (more functions for the position than for the field) and that such an element shows strain under a rigid rotation. The proof is ours.

Let us check on our quadrilateral with the field \(u = 10^{-3}(x + y/2)\), \(v = 10^{-3}(x/2 + y)\). The nodal displacements are \(u_{\mathrm{i}} = (0;\ 0{,}04;\ 0{,}051;\ 0{,}016)\) mm and \(v_{\mathrm{i}} = (0;\ 0{,}02;\ 0{,}048;\ 0{,}026)\) mm, and \(\mat B\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) gives at the points \((0, 0)\), \((-1, -1)\), \((1, 1)\) and \((0{,}5; -0{,}7)\) everywhere \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 10^{-3}\) to the tenth place (num-05.out, part D). For the triangle this is lemma 15.8. Here the same holds for a distorted quadrilateral because the element uses the same functions for position and for field: it is a matter of choice, not a general property of interpolation.

Lemma 15.36 Compatibility of isoparametric elements along a shared side (skladnost izoparametričnih elementov na stiku)

Let two elements Q4 have a shared side with nodes \(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\vek p_{\mathrm{b}}\) and displacements \(\vek u_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\vek u_{\mathrm{b}}\) at these nodes. Then their sides coincide as sets of points and the displacement fields have the same value at every point of this side.

Proof

We must show that the side and the field on it do not depend on the element.

  1. By lemma 15.29, point 3, on the side \(\eta = -1\) of the first element \(N_3 = N_4 = 0\) and \(N_1 = (1 - \xi)/2\), \(N_2 = (1 + \xi)/2\). With a numbering in which the shared side is exactly this one, the position is therefore \(\vek x = \tfrac{1 - \xi}{2}\vek p_{\mathrm{a}} + \tfrac{1 + \xi}{2}\vek p_{\mathrm{b}}\) and the displacement \(\vek u_{\mathrm{h}} = \tfrac{1 - \xi}{2}\vek u_{\mathrm{a}} + \tfrac{1 + \xi}{2}\vek u_{\mathrm{b}}\). The side is the segment from \(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}}\) to \(\vek p_{\mathrm{b}}\) and the field on it is an affine function of the position along the segment.
  2. For another side or another element with the same side the computation is the same, with the roles of the nodes possibly exchanged, which means the replacement \(\xi \to -\xi\). The segment and the affine field between the values \(\vek u_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\vek u_{\mathrm{b}}\) remain the same.
  3. The points of the segment are therefore the same in both elements and the values of the fields are equal at each, because an affine function on a segment is determined by the values at its ends.

Source: The lemma is not from a source. COOK, section 6.13, PDF pp. 252 to 253, states the requirement of compatibility for convergence, not a proof for Q4.

By lemma 15.36 the field on a mesh of quadrilaterals is continuous across the shared sides, and by theorem 15.32 the change of variables theorem holds on every element, so also the sum of the energies over the elements and the theorems on piecewise smooth fields of section 15.2. This answers the third question of the introduction.

15.5.6 The conductivity matrix of the quadrilateral

Section 15.3 used for the Q4 mesh a row of the conductivity matrix without derivation. Now we have all the ingredients. For a scalar field (temperature) the element Q4 replaces the matrix \(\mat B\) of equation (15.27) by a gradient row, and the element matrix is as for the triangle (lemma 15.17) the integral \((\mat k_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = \int k\,\nabla N_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\nabla N_{\mathrm{j}}\,t\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Lemma 15.37 The conductivity matrix of the four-node element on a square (prevodnostna matrika štirikotnika na kvadratu)

Let the element Q4 be a square with side \(h\), conductivity \(k\) and thickness \(t\), everything constant, with the nodes at the corners. Then

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{k\,t}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 & 4 & -1 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{15.29}\]

independent of \(h\). For a mesh of congruent squares with side \(h\) the row of the assembled matrix at an interior node \(I\) is \(\tfrac{k\,t}{3}\big(8\,T_{\mathrm{I}} - \sum_{\mathrm{J}} T_{\mathrm{J}}\big)\), where the sum runs over the eight neighbouring nodes.

Proof

We must show the element matrix and the row after assembly.

  1. For \(x = x_0 + h\,(1 + \xi)/2\) and \(y = y_0 + h\,(1 + \eta)/2\) we have \(\mat F = (h/2)\,\mat I\) and \(J = h^2/4\). By equation (15.26), \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x = \tfrac{2}{h}\,\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial\xi = \tfrac{\xi_{\mathrm{i}}}{2h}\,(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)\) and \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y = \tfrac{\eta_{\mathrm{i}}}{2h}\,(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi)\).
  2. The entry is \((\mat k_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = k\,t\,\tfrac{h^2}{4}\cdot\tfrac{1}{4h^2}\int_{\mathrm{K}} \big[\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}}(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{j}}\eta) + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}}(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi)(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{j}}\xi)\big]\mathrm{d}A\). With \(\int_{-1}^{1}(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{j}}\eta)\,\mathrm{d}\eta = 2 + \tfrac23\eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}}\) (terms with \(\eta\) to the first power have integral zero) and theorem 4.9 the integral of the first term is \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot 2\,(2 + \tfrac23\eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}})\), of the second \(\eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot 2\,(2 + \tfrac23\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}})\). Together \((\mat k_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac{k\,t}{16}\,\big[4(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}} + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}}) + \tfrac83\,\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}}\eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}}\big]\), independent of \(h\).
  3. For \(i = j\), \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}} = \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}} = 1\) and the entry is \(\tfrac{k\,t}{16}(8 + \tfrac83) = \tfrac23\,k\,t\). For adjacent nodes (they differ in one coordinate) \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}} + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{j}}\eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{j}} = -1\), so \(-\tfrac{k\,t}{6}\). For opposite nodes the sum is \(-2\) and the product \(1\), so \(\tfrac{k\,t}{16}(-8 + \tfrac83) = -\tfrac13\,k\,t\). This is the matrix (15.29).
  4. An interior node belongs to four elements. By theorem 7.13 the diagonal entry is the sum \(4\cdot\tfrac23\,k\,t = \tfrac83\,k\,t\). Each of the four nodes along an edge shares two elements with \(I\), the entry is \(2\cdot(-\tfrac16)\,k\,t = -\tfrac13\,k\,t\). Each of the four diagonal neighbours shares one element, the entry is \(-\tfrac13\,k\,t\) (opposite node). So the row is \(\tfrac{k\,t}{3}\,(8\,T_{\mathrm{I}} - \sum_{\mathrm{J}} T_{\mathrm{J}})\) with eight neighbours, the sum of the coefficients is \(0\) as for every conductivity matrix.

Source: COOK, section 6.2, PDF p. 222: the element for a scalar field is obtained from the structural one by renaming and compacting the matrices. The computations are ours (SymPy, num-05.out, part H).

The row in the lemma is exactly the one of section 15.3, derived now. A Q4 mesh differs from a mesh of triangles on the same squares. If we cut every square by a diagonal in the same direction, the two neighbours on the diagonal have coefficient zero, because the angles opposite the diagonal are right angles and their cotangent is zero (lemma 15.17, point 5), and each of the four neighbours along an edge has coefficient \(-k\,t\) (two angles of \(45^\circ\) with cotangents \(1\), \(-\tfrac12\,k\,t\cdot(1 + 1)\)), and the row is \(k\,t\,(4\,T_{\mathrm{I}} - \sum T_{\mathrm{J}})\). For Q4 all eight neighbours have a nonzero coefficient \(-\tfrac13\,k\,t\).

15.5.7 The eight-node element

The linear side of the quadrilateral is replaced by a quadratic one: each side gets one more node and the element has eight nodes, this is the element Q8. As in the quadratic bar element each side has three nodes, and we arrange the eight nodes in the square so that the corners \(1\) to \(4\) are as before and the midpoints of the sides \(5\) to \(8\) are on the axes \(\xi\) and \(\eta\).

Definition 15.38 The eight-node element (osemvozliščni element)

On the square \(K\) the nodes \((\xi_{\mathrm{i}}, \eta_{\mathrm{i}})\) are the corners \(1\) to \(4\) as for Q4 and the midpoints \(5 = (0, -1)\), \(6 = (1, 0)\), \(7 = (0, 1)\), \(8 = (-1, 0)\). The shape functions of the element Q8 are

\[N_{\mathrm{i}} = \tfrac14(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi)(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta - 1) \quad (i = 1, \dots, 4) ,\]
\[N_5 = \tfrac12(1 - \xi^2)(1 - \eta) , \; N_6 = \tfrac12(1 + \xi)(1 - \eta^2) , \; N_7 = \tfrac12(1 - \xi^2)(1 + \eta) , \; N_8 = \tfrac12(1 - \xi)(1 - \eta^2) . \tag{15.30}\]

The isoparametric element Q8 is the element of definition 15.30 with \(m = 8\).

Source: COOK, section 6.4, PDF pp. 227 and 228: the eight-node plane element, shape functions of equation (6.4-1) and their derivation by interpolation. COOK (PDF p. 229) calls this family "serendipity", the name is used in this book only here as a remark.

Lemma 15.39 Properties of the Q8 shape functions (lastnosti oblikovnih funkcij elementa Q8)

For the functions (15.30), \(N_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi_{\mathrm{j}}, \eta_{\mathrm{j}}) = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\). On the side \(\eta = -1\), \(N_3 = N_4 = N_6 = N_7 = N_8 = 0\) and \(N_1 = \xi(\xi - 1)/2\), \(N_5 = 1 - \xi^2\), \(N_2 = \xi(\xi + 1)/2\), so the same functions as for the quadratic bar element.

Proof

We must show three claims. The first by looking at where each function vanishes, the second by expanding a product, the third by inserting \(\eta = -1\).

  1. The function \(N_5\) vanishes where \(\xi = \pm 1\) (nodes \(1\) to \(4\), \(6\), \(8\)) or \(\eta = 1\) (node \(7\)), and at \((0, -1)\) it has the value \(\tfrac12\cdot 1\cdot 2 = 1\). Similarly for \(N_6\), \(N_7\), \(N_8\). The function \(N_1 = \tfrac14(1 - \xi)(1 - \eta)(-\xi - \eta - 1)\) vanishes at \(\xi = 1\) (nodes \(2\), \(3\), \(6\)) and \(\eta = 1\) (nodes \(3\), \(4\), \(7\)), at \((0, -1)\) and \((-1, 0)\) the third factor is zero, and at \((-1, -1)\) it is \(\tfrac14\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 1 = 1\). For \(N_2\), \(N_3\), \(N_4\) the computation is the same with the roles exchanged.
  2. The sum. For \(a = \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi\) and \(b = \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta\), \((1 + a)(1 + b)(a + b - 1) = a^2 + b^2 - 1 + ab + a^2 b + a b^2\). In the sum over the four corners the terms with odd powers of \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) or \(\eta_{\mathrm{i}}\) (\(ab\), \(a^2b\), \(ab^2\)) vanish, because \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\xi_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\eta_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) and all sign combinations occur once. What remains is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}\le 4} N_{\mathrm{i}} = \xi^2 + \eta^2 - 1\).
  3. Midpoints: \(N_5 + N_7 = \tfrac12(1 - \xi^2)\big[(1 - \eta) + (1 + \eta)\big] = 1 - \xi^2\) and \(N_6 + N_8 = 1 - \eta^2\). Together \(\xi^2 + \eta^2 - 1 + 1 - \xi^2 + 1 - \eta^2 = 1\).
  4. At \(\eta = -1\) we insert: \(N_5 = 1 - \xi^2\), \(N_7 = 0\), \(N_6 = N_8 = 0\) (factor \(1 - \eta^2 = 0\)), \(N_3 = N_4 = 0\) (factor \(1 + \eta = 0\)), \(N_1 = \tfrac14(1 - \xi)\cdot 2\cdot(-\xi) = \xi(\xi - 1)/2\) and \(N_2 = \xi(\xi + 1)/2\).

Source: The lemma is not from a source. The functions along a side are ONATE1, equation (3.11), PDF p. 103, as chapter 7 cites them.

For Q8 lemmas 15.35 and 15.36 also hold (with the same proof, three nodes on a side instead of two), but the condition of theorem 15.32 does not carry over to Q8. For Q4 the \(J\) is affine, for Q8 it is not: for the element with corners \((0, 0)\), \((40, 0)\), \((36, 30)\), \((4, 24)\) mm and midpoints \((20, -6)\), \((38, 15)\), \((20, 27)\), \((2, 12)\) mm, \(J = 297 + 30\,\xi - 33\,\eta - 42\,\xi^2 - 6\,\xi^2\eta\) mm² (SymPy, num-05.out, part I). A check at the corners is therefore not enough. We check the values of \(J\) on a \(201 \times 201\) grid of points (smallest value \(186\) mm², num-05.out, part E) or, like COOK, at the points where we will integrate (section 15.6). Such a check is no proof that \(J > 0\) everywhere, so theorem 15.32 is not proved for Q8.

One thing we can prove, and it is close to a shortcut that is often used with Q8: pushing the midside node of a side toward the corner.

Lemma 15.40 A side of the Q8 element and the position of the midside node (stranica elementa Q8 in lega srednjega vozlišča)

Let a side of the element Q8 have nodes \(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(\vek p_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(\vek p_{\mathrm{b}}\) (corner, midside node, corner), let \(\vek e = \vek p_{\mathrm{b}} - \vek p_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\vek p_{\mathrm{m}} = \tfrac12(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}} + \vek p_{\mathrm{b}}) + s\,\tfrac12\vek e\) for a number \(s\), so \(\tfrac{1 + s}{2}\) is the fraction of the length from \(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}}\) to \(\vek p_{\mathrm{m}}\) along \(\vek e\). The points of the side are \(\vek x(\tau) = \tfrac12(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}} + \vek p_{\mathrm{b}}) + \tfrac12\vek e\,\big[\tau + s\,(1 - \tau^2)\big]\), \(\tau \in [-1, 1]\). Then:

  1. The tangent is \(\vek x'(\tau) = \tfrac12\vek e\,(1 - 2s\tau)\).
  2. If \(|s| < \tfrac12\), then \(1 - 2s\tau > 0\) on \([-1, 1]\) and the tangent does not vanish. At \(s = \mp\tfrac12\), \(\vek x'(\mp 1) = \vek 0\), the tangent vanishes at one corner. For \(|s| > \tfrac12\) the tangent changes direction at the point \(\tau = 1/(2s) \in (-1, 1)\).
  3. For \(s = -0{,}6\) the points \(\tau = -1\) and \(\tau = -\tfrac23\) have the same position.
Proof

We must show three claims. The first by differentiating, the second by the sign of a factor, the third by solving a quadratic equation.

  1. By lemma 15.39, on the side \(\vek x = \vek p_{\mathrm{a}}\,\tfrac{\tau(\tau - 1)}{2} + \vek p_{\mathrm{m}}\,(1 - \tau^2) + \vek p_{\mathrm{b}}\,\tfrac{\tau(\tau + 1)}{2}\). We insert \(\vek p_{\mathrm{m}}\) and collect: \(\tfrac12(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}} + \vek p_{\mathrm{b}}) + \tfrac12\vek e\,\tau + \tfrac12 s\,\vek e\,(1 - \tau^2)\), which is the form in the statement. The derivative with respect to \(\tau\) is \(\tfrac12\vek e\,(1 - 2s\tau)\).
  2. The factor \(1 - 2s\tau\) is affine in \(\tau\), so it is positive on \([-1, 1]\) exactly when it is positive at both ends, that is \(1 - 2s > 0\) and \(1 + 2s > 0\), so \(|s| < \tfrac12\). At \(s = -\tfrac12\) the factor at \(\tau = -1\) equals \(1 + 2s = 0\), at \(s = \tfrac12\) at \(\tau = 1\) it equals \(1 - 2s = 0\). For \(|s| > \tfrac12\) the factor has the zero \(\tau = 1/(2s)\) inside \((-1, 1)\) and changes sign there, and with it the direction of the tangent.
  3. For \(s = -0{,}6\) the coordinate along \(\vek e\) is \(\tfrac12[\tau - 0{,}6\,(1 - \tau^2)]\). The value at \(\tau = -1\) is \(-\tfrac12\), so equal to that at \(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}}\). The equation \(\tau - 0{,}6\,(1 - \tau^2) = -1\) gives \(0{,}6\,\tau^2 + \tau + 0{,}4 = 0\) with solutions \(\tau = (-1 \pm 0{,}2)/1{,}2\), so \(-1\) and \(-\tfrac23\). The smallest value of the coordinate is at \(\tau = -\tfrac56\) and it is \(-\tfrac{61}{120}\) of the length \(|\vek e|\), so the side went \(\tfrac1{60}\) of half the length beyond the corner.

Source: ONATE1, section 6.1, PDF p. 211: for a quadratic element the side nodes must lie within the "middle third" of the distance between adjacent corners (the source states the condition for positive \(J\) without proof). COOK, section 6.11, PDF p. 250, figure 6.11-2b: node \(7\) moved to corner \(3\) gives a negative \(J\) at a Gauss point. Our condition \(|s| < \tfrac12\), a fraction between \(\tfrac14\) and \(\tfrac34\), is necessary for a tangent without a zero on the side and is weaker than the "middle third" condition, which corresponds to \(|s| < \tfrac13\).

Let us look at the figure for a side with ends \(x = \mp 1\) (the unit is half the side) and the midside node at \(s\). The axes are \(\tau\) horizontally and the coordinate \(x\) along the side vertically, the dashed verticals and horizontals are the ends \(\mp 1\). The straight line at \(s = 0\) is the uniform map, the midside node is in the middle. At \(s = -0{,}5\) the midside node is at a quarter of the distance from \(\vek p_{\mathrm{a}}\) and the curve has a horizontal tangent at \(\tau = -1\): the coordinate does not change there. At \(s = -0{,}6\) the curve goes below the value at the end and then returns, so that the points \(\tau = -1\) and \(\tau = -\tfrac23\) land in the same place: the side folds back onto itself.

The same happens in the plane. For a \(40 \times 30\) mm rectangle whose lower midside node is at \(x_{\mathrm{m}}\) mm instead of at \(20\), \(J(-1, -1) = 30\,(x_{\mathrm{m}} - 10)\) and \(J(1, -1) = 30\,(30 - x_{\mathrm{m}})\) mm². At \(x_{\mathrm{m}} = 20, 15, 10, 8\) mm, \(J(-1, -1) = 300, 150, 0, -60\) mm² and \(J(1, -1) = 300, 450, 600, 660\) mm² (num-05.out, part E). At \(x_{\mathrm{m}} = 10\), that is at a quarter of the side length, \(J\) at the corner is zero. The reason: the left and right sides are vertical, so \(x_\eta = 0\) at both lower corners and \(J = x_\xi\,y_\eta\), with \(y_\eta = 15\) mm and \(x_\xi = 20\,(1 - 2s\tau)\) by lemma 15.40 (with \(\vek e = (40, 0)\) mm and \(s = (x_{\mathrm{m}} - 20)/20\)). At \(\tau = -1\) this is \(2x_{\mathrm{m}} - 20\), at \(\tau = 1\) it is \(60 - 2x_{\mathrm{m}}\).

The following sections continue with three facts of this section. The matrix \(\mat B\) has \(J\) in the denominator, so the integrand of the stiffness matrix is a rational function and cannot be integrated as a polynomial (section 15.6). The field contains the linear fields and is compatible across the shared sides, so the element must pass the patch test (section 15.7). In space the same recipe is repeated with the brick, the image of the cube (section 15.10), except that a check at the corners is not enough there.

15.6 Gauss rules for elements and spurious modes (Gaussova pravila za elemente in lažni načini)

For the four-node element of section 15.5 take a concrete example: a steel quadrilateral with nodes \((0, 0)\), \((40, 0)\), \((36, 30)\) and \((4, 24)\) mm, thickness \(t = 10\) mm, with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\) in plane stress (theorem 11.33). We have to compute the stiffness matrix of this element as an integral, and here we meet a difficulty that the bar did not have.

The map of the square \([-1, 1]^2\) onto the quadrilateral (definition 15.30) has, by lemma 15.31, a determinant \(J\) that is linear in \(\xi\) and \(\eta\). For our quadrilateral \(J = 243 + 30\,\xi - 27\,\eta\) mm², which gives \(240\), \(300\), \(246\) and \(186\) mm² at the corners (num-06.out, part H). Since \(J > 0\) everywhere, the quadrilateral is a curved box in the plane (theorem 15.32), and by theorem 4.59

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = t \int_{[-1,1]^2} \mat B^\T\,\mat C\,\mat B\,J\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{15.31}\]

Every component of the matrix \(\mat B\) (definition 15.21) is a derivative of a shape function with respect to \(x\) or \(y\). By the chain rule it is a combination of the derivatives with respect to \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) with the inverse of the \(2 \times 2\) matrix of partial derivatives of the map, and this inverse is the adjugate matrix divided by \(J\). The integrand in equation (15.31) therefore has the form \((\text{polynomial})/J\), not a polynomial. A word on notation: \(\mat B\) is here the bold matrix of the element, whereas \(\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\) of chapter 7 is the row of the bar, \(\mat C\) is the material matrix of definition 3.18 (ONATE1 and COOK write it \(\mat D\) and \(\mat E\)), \(t\) is the thickness (not time), \(A\) the area of the element (for the bar a cross-section), and \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\) is always an area coordinate with an index (a length \(L\) elsewhere in the book has none).

For the bar we replaced such integrals by a weighted sum which, for some points \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\), has the form \(\sum w_{\mathrm{i}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\) (definition 7.24). We obtained the points for \(q = 1, 2, 3\) by demanding exactness for the powers \(1, \xi, \dots, \xi^{2q-1}\), and lemma 7.25 checked it. For larger \(q\) chapter 7 only stated that the rule exists (ONATE1, PDF p. 113). Here we prove it, because we need the statement for every \(q\): the number of points decides how much work every element costs, and whether the element stands firmly at all, as we shall see with spurious modes.

The idea of the proof in words. We have \(q\) points and \(q\) weights, so \(2q\) free numbers, and with them we would like to hit the polynomials up to degree \(2q - 1\). We divide a polynomial of degree \(2q - 1\) by a polynomial \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) of degree \(q\) whose roots are exactly the chosen points. The quotient and the remainder have degree at most \(q - 1\). The remainder is integrated exactly by every rule with \(q\) points and the right weights. The product of \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) with the quotient, however, is zero at the chosen points, so the rule gives zero for it, and its integral must be zero too. This is true if \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) is orthogonal to all polynomials of lower degree. So the points are the roots of such a polynomial. What "orthogonal" means we say for functions on \([-1, 1]\) with the inner product \((f, g) = \int_{-1}^{1} f\,g\,\mathrm{d}\xi\) (definition 6.16): \(f\) and \(g\) are orthogonal if \((f, g) = 0\).

Theorem 15.41 Gauss quadrature with \(q\) points (Gaussovo pravilo s \(q\) točkami)

Let \(q\) be a natural number and \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{n}}\) the set of polynomials of one variable of degree at most \(n\) (definition 1.63).

  1. There is exactly one polynomial \(p_{\mathrm{q}}(\xi) = \xi^q + c_{\mathrm{q}-1}\,\xi^{q-1} + \dots + c_0\) for which \(\int_{-1}^{1} p_{\mathrm{q}}\,s\,\mathrm{d}\xi = 0\) for every \(s \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{q}-1}\).
  2. The polynomial \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) has \(q\) distinct real roots \(\xi_1 < \dots < \xi_{\mathrm{q}}\) and all of them lie in the open interval \((-1, 1)\).
  3. Let \(\ell_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi) = \prod_{\mathrm{j} \ne \mathrm{i}} \dfrac{\xi - \xi_{\mathrm{j}}}{\xi_{\mathrm{i}} - \xi_{\mathrm{j}}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = \int_{-1}^{1} \ell_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}\xi\). Then \(\int_{-1}^{1} g\,\mathrm{d}\xi = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{q} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\) for every \(g \in \mathcal{P}_{2\mathrm{q}-1}\), and all weights are positive.
  4. No rule with \(q\) points \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\) and arbitrary weights \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) is exact for all polynomials of degree \(2q\). For the points \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\) of item 3 the polynomial \(p_{\mathrm{q}}^{\,2}\) fails.
Proof

We have to show four claims. First we find \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) as the solution of a linear system, then the roots by contradiction, then we divide a polynomial, and last we find a polynomial for which the rule fails.

  1. The inner product \((f, g) = \int_{-1}^{1} f\,g\,\mathrm{d}\xi\) has properties 1 to 4 of definition 6.16. The proof is the same as for the interval \([0, L]\) in chapter 6, only the interval differs. The functions \(1, \xi, \dots, \xi^{q-1}\) are linearly independent by lemma 6.23 (the proof with derivatives at \(0\) holds on \([-1, 1]\) too). The matrix \(G_{\mathrm{kj}} = \int_{-1}^{1} \xi^{k+j}\,\mathrm{d}\xi\) with \(k, j = 0, \dots, q-1\) is therefore positive definite by lemma 6.28, item 3, so it has an inverse.
  2. The condition of item 1 for \(s = \xi^k\) reads \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} G_{\mathrm{kj}}\,c_{\mathrm{j}} = -\int_{-1}^{1} \xi^{k+q}\,\mathrm{d}\xi\) for \(k = 0, \dots, q-1\). Since the integral is linear (lemma 3.39, item 1), it suffices to check the condition for these powers, because every \(s \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{q}-1}\) is a linear combination of them. A system with an invertible matrix has exactly one solution \(c_0, \dots, c_{\mathrm{q}-1}\), which is item 1.
  3. An auxiliary fact: if \(p(c) = 0\), then \(p(\xi) = (\xi - c)\,h(\xi)\) with a polynomial \(h\) of degree one lower. The reason is \(\xi^k - c^k = (\xi - c)(\xi^{k-1} + c\,\xi^{k-2} + \dots + c^{k-1})\), which we use on every term of \(p(\xi) - p(c)\). A nonzero polynomial of degree \(d\) therefore has at most \(d\) roots, since every root lowers the degree by one. So \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) has finitely many roots.
  4. Item 2. Let \(c_1 < \dots < c_{\mathrm{m}}\) be those roots of \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) in \((-1, 1)\) at which \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) changes sign (\(m \ge 0\)), and \(\pi(\xi) = (\xi - c_1) \cdots (\xi - c_{\mathrm{m}})\) (\(\pi = 1\) for \(m = 0\)). The product \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\,\pi\) does not change sign on \((-1, 1)\): at every \(c_{\mathrm{i}}\) both factors change sign and the changes cancel, elsewhere it is continuous and cannot change sign between two consecutive zeros, because it would have a zero in between (intermediate value theorem). The product is not identically zero and is continuous, so \(\int_{-1}^{1} p_{\mathrm{q}}\,\pi\,\mathrm{d}\xi \neq 0\): at a point where it differs from zero it is, by continuity, at least half of that value in absolute value on a small interval, which by lemma 3.39, items 3 and 4, gives a positive contribution, and elsewhere it has the same sign.
  5. If \(m < q\), then \(\pi \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{q}-1}\) and by item 1 we would have \(\int_{-1}^{1} p_{\mathrm{q}}\,\pi\,\mathrm{d}\xi = 0\), a contradiction with step 4. So \(m \ge q\), and since \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) has at most \(q\) roots by step 3, \(m = q\). Hence \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) has exactly \(q\) distinct real roots \(\xi_1, \dots, \xi_{\mathrm{q}}\) in \((-1, 1)\). The difference \(p_{\mathrm{q}} - (\xi - \xi_1) \cdots (\xi - \xi_{\mathrm{q}})\) has degree less than \(q\) and \(q\) roots, so by step 3 it is zero, and \(p_{\mathrm{q}} = \prod_{\mathrm{i}} (\xi - \xi_{\mathrm{i}})\). This is item 2.
  6. Item 3. The denominators in \(\ell_{\mathrm{i}}\) are not zero, because the roots are distinct. We have \(\ell_{\mathrm{i}} \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{q}-1}\) and \(\ell_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi_{\mathrm{j}}) = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). For every \(r \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{q}-1}\) the polynomial \(r - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} r(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,\ell_{\mathrm{i}}\) has degree at most \(q - 1\) and \(q\) roots \(\xi_{\mathrm{j}}\), so by step 3 it is zero. By linearity of the integral, \(\int_{-1}^{1} r\,\mathrm{d}\xi = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,r(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\) for every \(r \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{q}-1}\).
  7. Let \(g \in \mathcal{P}_{2\mathrm{q}-1}\) and \(r = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,\ell_{\mathrm{i}} \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{q}-1}\). The polynomial \(g - r\) has the roots \(\xi_1, \dots, \xi_{\mathrm{q}}\). By step 3, \(g - r = (\xi - \xi_1)\,h_1\), and since \(\xi_2 - \xi_1 \neq 0\) we have \(h_1(\xi_2) = 0\) and \(h_1 = (\xi - \xi_2)\,h_2\). Repeating the procedure, \(g - r = p_{\mathrm{q}}\,s\) with a polynomial \(s\) of degree at most \((2q - 1) - q = q - 1\).
  8. Then \(\int_{-1}^{1} g\,\mathrm{d}\xi = \int_{-1}^{1} p_{\mathrm{q}}\,s\,\mathrm{d}\xi + \int_{-1}^{1} r\,\mathrm{d}\xi = \int_{-1}^{1} r\,\mathrm{d}\xi\) by item 1, because \(s \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{q}-1}\). The sum is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,\big(p_{\mathrm{q}}(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,s(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}) + r(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\big) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,r(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\), because \(p_{\mathrm{q}}(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}) = 0\). By step 6 this is \(\int_{-1}^{1} r\,\mathrm{d}\xi\). The two sides are equal.
  9. Weights. The polynomial \(\ell_{\mathrm{i}}^{\,2}\) has degree \(2q - 2 \le 2q - 1\), so by step 8 \(\int_{-1}^{1} \ell_{\mathrm{i}}^{\,2}\,\mathrm{d}\xi = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} w_{\mathrm{j}}\,\ell_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi_{\mathrm{j}})^2 = w_{\mathrm{i}}\). The integral of the nonnegative continuous polynomial \(\ell_{\mathrm{i}}^{\,2}\), which equals \(1\) at \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\), is positive (as in step 4), so \(w_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\). This is item 3.
  10. Item 4. Let \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\) be arbitrary points, \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) arbitrary weights and \(\omega(\xi) = \prod_{\mathrm{i}} (\xi - \zeta_{\mathrm{i}})\). The polynomial \(\omega^2\) has degree \(2q\), is nonnegative and has at most \(q\) roots (step 3), so \(\int_{-1}^{1} \omega^2\,\mathrm{d}\xi > 0\) as in step 4. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,\omega(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}})^2\) is zero, because \(\omega(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}) = 0\). For \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) we have \(\omega = p_{\mathrm{q}}\).

Source: KREYSZIG, section 19.5, PDF p. 863: Gauss showed exactness up to degree \(2n - 1\), the nodes are the zeros of the Legendre polynomial \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\), and the coefficients are obtained from Lagrange's interpolation polynomial. COOK, section 6.3, PDF p. 224: the points are roots of Legendre polynomials. ONATE1, PDF p. 113: degree \(2q - 1\). The proof in steps 1 to 10 is not from the sources, they do not contain it. The polynomial \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) is the Legendre polynomial divided by its leading coefficient (SymPy, num-06.out, part A).

The theorem has shown that the rule exists for every \(q\), that the points are the roots of \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\), and that nothing better is possible: with \(q\) points we never hit degree \(2q\), whatever the choice, so \(2q - 1\) is the highest degree that can be reached. What the polynomials \(p_{\mathrm{q}}\) look like is shown in figure 15.23. They are drawn as \(p_{\mathrm{q}}(\xi)/p_{\mathrm{q}}(1)\), so that all have the value \(1\) at \(\xi = 1\) and can be compared. The polynomial \(p_1 = \xi\) has the root \(0\), the only point of the one-point rule with weight \(2\). The polynomial \(p_2 = \xi^2 - \tfrac13\) has the roots \(\pm 1/\sqrt3\), as in definition 7.24. The polynomial \(p_3\) has the roots \(0\) and \(\pm\sqrt{3/5}\), and for \(q = 1, 2, 3\) the computation from the proof (SymPy, num-06.out, part A) gives the weights \(2\), \(1\) and \(1\), \(5/9\) and \(8/9\), exactly those of chapter 7. Only the polynomial \(p_4\) with roots \(\pm 0{,}3400\) and \(\pm 0{,}8611\) (weights \(0{,}6521\) and \(0{,}3479\)) and the polynomial \(p_5\) with roots \(0\), \(\pm 0{,}5385\) and \(\pm 0{,}9062\) (weights \(0{,}5689\), \(0{,}4786\) and \(0{,}2369\)) are new. The roots of each polynomial are the Gauss points, all of them lie inside the end points and crowd more towards them.

For a plane element we have two coordinates. It suffices to use the rule in each, one after the other, as the next corollary says.

Corollary 15.42 Gauss rule on the square and cube (Gaussovo pravilo na kvadratu in kocki)

Let \(g(\xi, \eta)\) be a polynomial of two variables of degree at most \(2n - 1\) in \(\xi\) and at most \(2m - 1\) in \(\eta\). Let \((\xi_{\mathrm{a}}, w_{\mathrm{a}})\) be the points and weights of the rule with \(n\) points and \((\eta_{\mathrm{b}}, v_{\mathrm{b}})\) of the rule with \(m\) points from theorem 15.41. Then

\[\int_{[-1,1]^2} g\,\mathrm{d}A = \sum_{\mathrm{a}=1}^{n} \sum_{\mathrm{b}=1}^{m} w_{\mathrm{a}}\,v_{\mathrm{b}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{a}}, \eta_{\mathrm{b}}) . \tag{15.32}\]

The same holds for a polynomial of three variables on the cube \([-1, 1]^3\) with a triple sum.

Proof

We have to show that the double integral splits into two one-dimensional ones, and to use theorem 15.41 on each.

  1. By theorem 4.9 (the same in the plane), \(\int_{[-1,1]^2} g\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{-1}^{1} G(\eta)\,\mathrm{d}\eta\) with \(G(\eta) = \int_{-1}^{1} g(\xi, \eta)\,\mathrm{d}\xi\).
  2. For every \(\eta\) the function \(g(\cdot, \eta)\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(2n - 1\) in \(\xi\), so by item 3 of theorem 15.41 \(G(\eta) = \sum_{\mathrm{a}} w_{\mathrm{a}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{a}}, \eta)\).
  3. The function \(\eta \mapsto g(\xi_{\mathrm{a}}, \eta)\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(2m - 1\), and \(G\) is their linear combination with the weights \(w_{\mathrm{a}}\), so it is a polynomial of the same degree. By theorem 15.41, \(\int_{-1}^{1} G\,\mathrm{d}\eta = \sum_{\mathrm{b}} v_{\mathrm{b}}\,G(\eta_{\mathrm{b}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{b}} \sum_{\mathrm{a}} v_{\mathrm{b}}\,w_{\mathrm{a}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{a}}, \eta_{\mathrm{b}})\). For the cube we repeat the step once more.

Source: ONATE1, equation (6.39), PDF p. 221: a double sum with weights \(W_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(W_{\mathrm{q}}\), and the statement that the points and weights per coordinate come from table 3.1. The proof is not from the source.

For a rectangular four-node element with a 2D material this means the following. Let the element be a rectangle \(2a \times 2b\) with nodes at the corners, so \(x = a\,\xi\) and \(y = b\,\eta\) and \(J = ab\) is constant. The derivative of the shape function \(N_{\mathrm{i}} = \tfrac14(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi)(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)\) is \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x = \tfrac{\xi_{\mathrm{i}}}{4a}\,(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)\), linear in \(\eta\) and independent of \(\xi\), and \(\partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y = \tfrac{\eta_{\mathrm{i}}}{4b}\,(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi)\), linear in \(\xi\). Every term of the integrand \(\mat B^\T \mat C \mat B\,J\) is therefore a product of two such derivatives, so in each variable of degree at most \(2 \le 3 = 2 \cdot 2 - 1\). By corollary 15.42 the \(2 \times 2\) rule is exact. In the eight-node element (definition 15.38) the shape functions also have the terms \(\xi^2\), \(\eta^2\), \(\xi^2\eta\) and \(\xi\eta^2\). The derivative with respect to \(\xi\) is therefore a combination of \(1\), \(\xi\), \(\eta\), \(\xi\eta\) and \(\eta^2\), and the derivative with respect to \(\eta\) a combination of \(1\), \(\xi\), \(\eta\), \(\xi\eta\) and \(\xi^2\). A product of two derivatives has degree up to \(4\) in each variable, and since \(2n - 1 \ge 4\) holds only from \(n = 3\) on, the \(3 \times 3\) rule is exact. That the rule with one point fewer in each direction is not exact for either element is shown by the computation below and by the count of spurious modes (num-06.out, parts D and G). We call the smallest exact rule full integration.

Definition 15.43 Full integration (polna integracija)

The rule \(n \times n\) (in 3D \(n \times n \times n\)) for computing \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the full integration of an element if \(n\) is the smallest number of points for which the rule is exact for the integrand of the stiffness matrix in the form where \(J\) is constant (a rectangle, and for elements with side nodes these are at the midpoints of the sides). A rule with fewer points is reduced integration (reducirana integracija). For the four-node element full integration is \(2 \times 2\) and reduced \(1 \times 1\), for the eight-node element \(3 \times 3\) and \(2 \times 2\).

Source: COOK, section 6.8, PDF p. 237: "full integration" is a rule that exactly integrates all stiffness coefficients of an undistorted element, and "underintegration" is a rule of lower order. ONATE1, section 6.8, PDF p. 232: full or exact integration is the rule that exactly integrates the same expression for a rectangle or a straight-sided triangle.

Let us try it on an element \(40 \times 30\) mm with \(t = 10\) mm (SymPy, num-06.out, part D). The entry \(k_{11}\) is \(873\,504{,}27\) N/mm with the exact integral. The \(2 \times 2\) rule gives this value, the \(3 \times 3\) rule too (the difference in the largest entry of the matrix is below \(10^{-9}\) N/mm), since by corollary 15.42 both have enough points. The \(1 \times 1\) rule gives \(655\,128{,}21\) N/mm, exactly \(3/4\) of the true value. The reason is in the terms: \(k_{11}\) is the sum of two terms, each containing one of \((1 - \eta)^2\) and \((1 - \xi)^2\) (squares of the derivatives of \(N_1\) with respect to \(x\) and \(y\)) multiplied by constants. The exact integral is \(\int_{[-1,1]^2} (1 - \eta)^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 2 \cdot \tfrac83 = \tfrac{16}{3}\), the one-point rule at the centre gives \(4 \cdot 1 = 4\), a ratio of \(3/4\) for both terms. This is the case of corollary 15.42 with degree \(2\) against \(2n - 1 = 1\): the rule fails exactly at the term \(\eta^2\), which the full integration still captures.

For a general quadrilateral the situation changes. The square \([-1, 1]^2\) with the points of the rules \(1 \times 1\), \(2 \times 2\) and \(3 \times 3\) shows where the values of the integrand are taken, the coordinates \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) are as before. For our quadrilateral the integrand is \((\text{polynomial})/J\) and not a polynomial, so corollary 15.42 says nothing about the accuracy. A computation with the rules \(n \times n\) for \(n = 1, \dots, 5\) and a comparison with a very accurate computation (the \(12 \times 12\) rule, value \(k_{11} = 799\,129{,}02\) N/mm) gives the relative errors of the entry \(k_{11}\)

\(n\) 1 2 3 4 5
error \(2{,}9 \cdot 10^{-1}\) \(1{,}1 \cdot 10^{-3}\) \(4{,}0 \cdot 10^{-6}\) \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(5{,}7 \cdot 10^{-11}\)

(num-06.out, part E). Every extra point in each direction reduces the error by a factor of about \(270\). The cause is not proved in this section: the integrand is not a polynomial, because the denominator \(J\) is not constant. The zero of the denominator on \(\eta = 0\) is at \(\xi = -243/30 = -8{,}1\), outside the interval, and the polynomials of the rule imitate it badly only near it. For comparison take an element in which \(J\) changes along \(\xi\) in the ratio \(3 : 1\), so that the integrand is \(1/(1 + \xi/2)\) with the zero of the denominator at \(\xi = -2\). For \(\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{1 + \xi/2}\,\mathrm{d}\xi = 2\ln 3 = 2{,}19722\) the errors at \(q = 1, \dots, 5\) are \(-1{,}97 \cdot 10^{-1}\), \(-1{,}54 \cdot 10^{-2}\), \(-1{,}15 \cdot 10^{-3}\), \(-8{,}39 \cdot 10^{-5}\) and \(-6{,}09 \cdot 10^{-6}\) (mkk.out, part A), so it falls only by a factor of about \(13\) per point. A more distorted element, that is a nearer zero of the denominator, thus needs more points. The folded quadrilateral of section 15.5, where \(J\) is negative at one corner, is not covered by theorem 4.59 at all, so no rule computes an area integral there.

For a triangle we do not use the square but area coordinates \(L_1, L_2, L_3\) (definition 15.3), and the integral of a monomial is in lemma 15.9. The rule has points given by area coordinates and weights that are shares of the area \(A\).

Lemma 15.44 Quadrature rules for a triangle (pravila za trikotnik)

Let a triangle have area \(A\) and area coordinates \(L_1, L_2, L_3\) (definition 15.3). The rule \(R_1\) has one point \((\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)\) with weight \(A\). The rule \(R_2\) has three points \((\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)\) and the two others by cyclic exchange, each with weight \(A/3\) (midpoints of the sides). The rule \(R_3\) has three points \((\tfrac23, \tfrac16, \tfrac16)\) and the two others by cyclic exchange, each with weight \(A/3\). Then:

  1. All three rules integrate polynomials of degree at most \(1\) in \(x\) and \(y\) exactly. The rules \(R_2\) and \(R_3\) also integrate polynomials of degree \(2\) exactly, the rule \(R_1\) does not.
  2. The rules \(R_2\) and \(R_3\) fail at \(L_1^3\), the rule \(R_1\) at \(L_1^2\).
Proof

We have to show that the integrals of the monomials \(L_1^a L_2^b L_3^c\) are computed correctly, and then that this suffices for all polynomials.

  1. By lemma 15.9, \(\int L_1^a L_2^b L_3^c\,\mathrm{d}A = a!\,b!\,c!\,2A/(a + b + c + 2)!\). For degree \(1\) this is \(A/3\), for degree \(2\) \(\int L_1^2\,\mathrm{d}A = A/6\) and \(\int L_1 L_2\,\mathrm{d}A = A/12\).
  2. Degree 1. For \(L_1\) the rule \(R_1\) gives \(A \cdot \tfrac13\). The rules \(R_2\) and \(R_3\) give \(\tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + 0) = \tfrac{A}{3}\) and \(\tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac23 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac16) = \tfrac{A}{3}\), and by symmetry the same holds for \(L_2\) and \(L_3\).
  3. Degree 2. For \(R_2\): \(L_1^2\) gives \(\tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 + 0) = \tfrac{A}{6}\) and \(L_1 L_2\) gives \(\tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac14 + 0 + 0) = \tfrac{A}{12}\). For \(R_3\): \(L_1^2\) gives \(\tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac49 + \tfrac1{36} + \tfrac1{36}) = \tfrac{A}{6}\), and \(L_1 L_2\) gives \(\tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac16 + \tfrac16\cdot\tfrac23 + \tfrac16\cdot\tfrac16) = \tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac19 + \tfrac19 + \tfrac1{36}) = \tfrac{A}{12}\). For \(R_1\): \(L_1^2\) gives \(A/9 \neq A/6\).
  4. Degree 3. \(\int L_1^3\,\mathrm{d}A = A/10\). The rule \(R_2\) gives \(\tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac18 + \tfrac18) = \tfrac{A}{12}\), and the rule \(R_3\) gives \(\tfrac{A}{3}(\tfrac8{27} + \tfrac1{216} + \tfrac1{216}) = \tfrac{11A}{108}\). Both differ from \(A/10\).
  5. A general polynomial. The coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) are affine functions of the \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\) (lemma 15.4), so a polynomial of degree \(d\) in \(x\) and \(y\) is a linear combination of products of at most \(d\) coordinates \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\). A product with fewer than \(d\) factors we multiply by \((L_1 + L_2 + L_3)^{d - k} = 1\) and get a linear combination of monomials \(L_1^a L_2^b L_3^c\) with \(a + b + c = d\). All rules are linear in the function and the integral is linear, so it suffices to check these monomials. The monomials of degree \(2\) are \(L_{\mathrm{i}}^2\) and \(L_{\mathrm{i}} L_{\mathrm{j}}\), of degree \(1\) they are \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\), and \(L_2\), \(L_3\) give the same computations as \(L_1\) by the cyclic symmetry of the rules.

Source: ONATE1, section 6.4.2 and figure 6.5, PDF p. 222: the rule for a triangle in area coordinates, weights with sum \(1/2\) for the reference triangle, accuracy is the degree of the highest polynomial integrated exactly. The values are ours, checked in num-06.out, part B.

The points of the three rules are shown in the lower row of figure 15.24: the centroid, the midpoints of the sides and the interior points, each of which lies at the middle of the segment between one corner and the centroid, and the corners have \(L_1\), \(L_2\) and \(L_3\) equal to \(1\) respectively. The area coordinates are affine functions of \(x\) and \(y\) (lemma 15.4), so the midpoint of a segment has as its coordinates the average of the coordinates of the end points: the average of the corner \((1, 0, 0)\) and the centroid \((\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)\) is exactly \((\tfrac23, \tfrac16, \tfrac16)\).

In all this we did not ask what happens if the rule is reduced. If so, the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) contains only the information that the points of the rule see. Let us look at what this means for the motions of the element that they do not see.

Let the element have \(n\) degrees of freedom (the four-node plane element \(8\), the eight-node \(16\)) and let the rule have \(P\) points with weights \(W_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) (products of one-dimensional weights, positive by item 3 of theorem 15.41). The strain matrix at the point \(p\) is \(\mat B_{\mathrm{p}}\) of size \(3 \times n\) and \(J_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) is the determinant of the map in it, and

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \sum_{\mathrm{p}=1}^{P} W_{\mathrm{p}}\,t\,J_{\mathrm{p}}\,\mat B_{\mathrm{p}}^\T\,\mat C\,\mat B_{\mathrm{p}} . \tag{15.33}\]

The rigid motions in the plane, two translations and one rotation, three in all, have zero strain. For the triangle lemma 15.25 showed that there are no other motions without strain.

Definition 15.45 Spurious mode (lažni način)

Let \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the stiffness matrix of an element of order \(n\) from equation (15.33) and \(\vek d\) the column of nodal displacements of the element. The column \(\vek d\) is a spurious mode if \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) but the displacement field of the element determined by \(\vek d\) is not a rigid motion (a translation and a rotation of a rigid body). The name is "spurious" (false) because the element deforms under \(\vek d\) but needs no force for it and stores no energy, so it behaves as if the motion met no resistance. By lemma 7.16, \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) exactly when \(\vek d^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = 0\).

Source: COOK, section 6.8, PDF pp. 237 and 238: "spurious mode" (also "zero-energy deformation mode", "hourglass mode", "mechanism"): an element with it has no resistance to nodal forces that excite it. The proof and the expressions are not from the source, the name in Slovenian is ours.

Lemma 15.46 Number of spurious modes under reduced integration (število lažnih načinov pri reducirani integraciji)

Let \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the matrix of order \(n\) from equation (15.33) with \(\mat C\) positive definite, \(W_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) and \(J_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\). Then:

  1. \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) exactly when \(\mat B_{\mathrm{p}}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) at every point \(p\).
  2. The dimension of the kernel of \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is at least \(n - 3P\). The kernel contains three independent rigid motions, so the number of independent spurious modes, that is the dimension of the kernel minus \(3\) (the number of directions the kernel has besides the rigid motions), is at least \(n - 3P - 3\).
Proof

We have to show that the energy splits into contributions of the points and that the number of equations bounds the kernel.

  1. From equation (15.33), \(\vek d^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = \sum_{\mathrm{p}} W_{\mathrm{p}}\,t\,J_{\mathrm{p}}\,(\mat B_{\mathrm{p}}\vek d)^\T\,\mat C\,(\mat B_{\mathrm{p}}\vek d)\). Every term is nonnegative, because \(\mat C\) is positive definite, and zero exactly for \(\mat B_{\mathrm{p}}\vek d = \vek 0\), because \(W_{\mathrm{p}}\), \(t\), \(J_{\mathrm{p}}\) are positive. The sum is zero exactly when every term is zero. By lemma 7.16 this is equivalent to \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) (the matrix is symmetric and, by this computation, positive semidefinite).
  2. By step 1 the kernel is the set of solutions of the system \(\mat B_{\mathrm{p}}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) for \(p = 1, \dots, P\), which is \(3P\) homogeneous equations in \(n\) unknowns. Such a set of solutions has dimension at least \(n - 3P\) (every equation lowers the dimension by at most one).
  3. The displacements of a rigid motion correspond to the field \(\vek u = (a - \omega y,\ b + \omega x)\), which is linear and is therefore reproduced exactly by the element, by lemma 15.35. Its strain is zero everywhere, so it lies in the kernel. The three columns of the rigid motions (translation in the direction \(x\), translation in the direction \(y\), rotation) are independent.
