For the annulus of figure 15.29 the elements are distorted, the boundary is only partly clamped, and \(8\) fields remain, not \(0\), but the pressure does no work on any of them, so the mesh locks all the same (theorem 15.56, item 4). But the proof shows where the fault is: when the constraint is at four points, the element must have \(\alpha_3 = \beta_3 = 0\), that is no terms \(\xi\eta\), which are the ones that bend the element, as in figure 15.31.

15.8.6 Selective integration (izbirna integracija)

Let us look for a way out. The constraint \(\operatorname{div}\vek u_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) is required only by the penalty term, not by the term of shape. If we integrate it with fewer points, there will be fewer constraints, and the shape part keeps the full rule that we need for stability.

Definition 15.58 Selective integration (izbirna integracija)

Let a plane element have the matrix (15.41). Selective integration (izbirna integracija) computes the shape part \(\mat k_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{e}}\) with the full Gauss rule (for Q4 \(2 \times 2\)) and the volumetric part \(\mat k_{\mathrm{K},\mathrm{e}}\) with fewer points (for Q4 \(1 \times 1\), for Q8 \(2 \times 2\) instead of \(3 \times 3\)). A rule that chooses a different number of points for two parts of the same expression is called selective, because we choose which part gets which rule.

Source: COOK §13.5 (PDF pp. 513-515, read): "If \(n = m\) and sampling points \(i\) and \(j\) are the same, the integration scheme is uniform, otherwise it is selective." The definition in our form.

The system matrix is then \(G\,\mat K_{\mathrm{G}} + K\,\mat C_1^\T\mat C_1\) with the matrix \(\mat C_1\) that has rows only at these fewer points. This is again a system of theorem 15.56, only with a shorter matrix of constraints, and the theorem holds unchanged if hypothesis (H) holds: the only field with divergence zero at these points and with zero energy of shape is zero. This does not follow from the theorem, so in the computations of the table we checked that the reduced matrix of the system is positive definite (its smallest eigenvalue is positive, num-08.py). There are fewer constraints, so \(V_{\mathrm{c}}\) is larger. For the tube of the first paragraph the dimension \(8\) with the full rule grew to \(48\) with the one-point rule (the count above), and in the table the ratio at \(\nu = 0{,}4999\) is no longer \(0{,}1765\) but \(0{,}9955\). The limit as \(\nu \to \tfrac12\), the field \(\vek d^*/(E/3)\) of item 3 of the theorem, also gives the ratio \(0{,}9955\) (NumPy). The table also shows Q8 with the full rule for the shape part, \(3\times3\), and the volumetric part with \(2 \times 2\): the ratio is \(1{,}0000\) at all \(\nu\).

The price is that the volumetric term is no longer integrated exactly. For the element of figure 15.31 the energy of the volumetric part is \(\tfrac23\,K\,\kappa^2 a\,b^3\), and the one-point rule in the centre estimates it as zero, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\) there. The computed functional is no longer the energy of the body, so the estimate of theorem 6.39 of chapter 6 does not hold for it, as it speaks about the exactly integrated energy. The confidence in the result comes from the table, not from a theorem: \(0{,}9955\) for Q4. We do not claim that selective integration never fails: COOK (PDF p. 516, read) says that "reduced integration may have to be accompanied by an element stabilization device in order to avoid spurious modes", and section 15.6 shows that the Q8 element with the \(2\times2\) rule has four zero eigenvalues, so the shape part always gets the full rule. Elements with a mixed formulation (COOK PDF pp. 517-518) are a topic of their own and we only name them here.

15.8.7 Plane stress does not lock (ravninsko napetostno stanje ne zaklene)

Theorem 15.56 claims that \(K \to \infty\) causes locking. Let us test whether there is no locking without it. Take the same tube in plane stress, as if it were a thin plate with a hole (definition 11.32), with the same material, \(\nu = 0{,}4999\). The Q4 mesh with the full rule gives the ratio \(0{,}9940\), the Q8 mesh with the \(3\times3\) rule \(1{,}0000\) (num-08.py, Lamé solution of theorem 11.27 with \(S = 0\), \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(a) = 18{,}979\) µm). The mesh does not lock, although the material is the same.

The reason is corollary 11.34, item 2: plane stress of a material with \(E\), \(\nu\) solves the same plane system as plane strain with \(E_{\mathrm{p}} = E\,(1 + 2\nu)/(1 + \nu)^2\) and \(\nu_{\mathrm{p}} = \nu/(1 + \nu)\). At \(\nu = 0{,}4999\), \(\nu_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}33329\) and \(E_{\mathrm{p}} = 174{,}2\) GPa, so the bulk modulus of the replacement plane material is \(E_{\mathrm{p}}/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu_{\mathrm{p}})\big) = 174{,}2\) GPa, finite, and the shear modulus stays \(G = 65{,}34\) GPa. The ratio \(K_{\mathrm{p}}/G = 2{,}67\) is as small as for steel. Where is the volume? At \(\nu = 0{,}4999\) the true field has in the plane \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} + \varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = 1{,}2247 \cdot 10^{-4}\), but the plate becomes thinner, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -1{,}2242 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the sum of the three is \(4{,}9 \cdot 10^{-8}\): the thinning in the direction \(z\) takes over the volume that the plane must not change. Plane strain prevented this with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\). COOK (PDF p. 516, read) says the same: "For plane stress conditions, there is no locking or ill-conditioning even when \(\nu = 0{,}50\)." The hypothesis \(K \to \infty\) of theorem 15.56 therefore does not hold for plane stress, and neither does the conclusion, the constraints \(\operatorname{div}\vek u_{\mathrm{h}} \to 0\).

15.8.8 The same phenomenon in bar and beam (isti pojav pri palici in nosilcu)

The locking that we found is not new. Chapter 6 chose for the hanging bar in space the family of fields \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), which does not allow thinning, and obtained the ratio \(E/(\lambda + 2\mu) = (1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)/(1 - \nu) = 0{,}7429\) at \(\nu = 0{,}3\). That is a constraint chosen by the family of fields, not by the mesh: at \(\nu = 0{,}4999\) the ratio is \(0{,}0006\) (num-08.py), and as \(K \to \infty\) it points to the same compulsion. For the Timoshenko beam (lemma 12.35) the penalty number is \(kGA\), the constraint is the shear strain at the Gauss points, with the full rule, \(2\) points per element, only zero remains (lemma 12.36), and with one point bending stays free (lemma 12.37). Here the penalty number is \(K/G\), the constraint the divergence, the full \(2\times2\) rule for Q4 leaves only zero (theorem 15.57), and the one-point rule allows bending. For axisymmetric elements (section 15.9) the volumetric strain is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \varepsilon_{\theta\theta}\) and the same theorem and the same remedy apply, for three-dimensional elements (section 15.10) the constraint is of the same kind, and COOK (PDF p. 515, read) gives \(3/1\) as the favourable ratio for the trilinear element with one point.

Locking is therefore not a fault of the mesh but the consequence of two things: a large number in the material and too small a space of fields that can carry that number. We remove it by the choice of the rule, at the cost of one of these two. The table shows that at \(\nu\) near \(\tfrac12\) the eight-node element with the \(2\times2\) rule for the volumetric part and \(3\times3\) for the shape part computes the tube to four decimals, and the four-node one with one point to half a percent.

15.9 Axisymmetric elements (osnosimetrični elementi)

The tube with radii 40 mm and 60 mm from chapter 11 has a closed solution, Lamé's (theorem 11.27). A piston, a wheel, the head of a pressure vessel or a valve body have the same kind of shape but no closed solution. Must we therefore cut them into thousands of three-dimensional elements? No, if the body is a solid of revolution (vrtenina), a body made by turning a plane region about an axis, and the load is the same all around the axis: then a mesh of its cross section is enough, a plane mesh as in sections 15.4 and 15.5. The word "axisymmetric" says that the body and its load can be turned about the axis without changing (symmetry about an axis), and the element is here a ring, because we get it by turning a plane element about the axis, like a hoop.

The model is the following (figure 15.33 shows the body). The body is isotropic, homogeneous and linearly elastic with small strains (theorem 3.11), steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\). Its shape is a solid of revolution about the axis \(z\), the loads are pressures on the surfaces of revolution and forces that do not change when turned about the axis, and so are the supports. Real bodies violate this with bolt holes, a side force and vibration that is not axisymmetric (COOK, PDF p. 523). We do not allow torsion, which chapter 16 treats.

We make the solid of revolution as follows. In the plane \((r, z)\) we take the section (meridional section, meridianski presek), a region \(\Omega\) at \(r > 0\) that the mesh cuts into quadrilaterals. The axis \(z\) is the dashed vertical line and the radius \(r\) is the distance from it, for our element \(40\) mm. When we turn one quadrilateral \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\) with its four nodes through the angle \(\theta\) about the axis, we get a ring that has the same section at every angle. Each node is then a circle, not a point.

This figure fixes what an "axisymmetric field" means. If we turn the loaded body through any angle about the axis, we get the same body with the same load, and the equations of an isotropic material do not change under the turn. The turned displacement field is therefore a solution of the same problem, and if the supports allow no rigid motion, it equals the original by theorem 11.4. This means that the radial and axial components of the displacement are the same at all angles. The circumferential component must be zero: a reflection in a plane through the axis leaves the load unchanged, but it changes the sign of the circumferential displacement, so it equals its own opposite. For bodies without supports this holds up to a rigid motion. In the definition we take this as the model, which holds for Lamé's tube and sphere of chapter 11.

Definition 15.59 Axisymmetric state (osnosimetrično stanje)

Let \(\Omega\) be an open set in the plane \((r, z)\) at \(r > 0\), and let the body \(K\) be the image of the set \(D = \{(r, \theta, z)\colon (r, z) \in \Omega,\ \theta_0 < \theta < \theta_0 + 2\pi\}\) under cylindrical coordinates (lemma 11.15), with the cut at \(\theta = \theta_0\) added. The displacement field \(\vek u\) of the body \(K\) is an axisymmetric state (osnosimetrično stanje) if in the local basis of cylindrical coordinates it has the form

\[\vek u = u_{\mathrm{r}}(r, z)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} + u_{\mathrm{z}}(r, z)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} , \tag{15.43}\]

where \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuously differentiable functions of two variables on \(\Omega\), and the circumferential component is zero. We assume here that the load (forces on the surface and in the body) is axisymmetric too: its local components \(b_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(b_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(t_{\mathrm{z}}\) are functions of \((r, z)\) only and the circumferential ones are zero.

Source: ONATE1 §7.2.1 (PDF p. 249-250), COOK §14.1 (PDF p. 522). The form of the definition after plane strain, definition 11.30, is ours.

In an axisymmetric state there is one strain that a plane element does not have: the circumferential one. We take a circle of points of the body with radius \(r\) about the axis, a hoop (kolobar), seen from above, that is a fibre of the body. Its length is \(2\pi r\). When every point moves radially by \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\), the hoop has the new radius \(r + u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the length \(2\pi(r + u_{\mathrm{r}})\), so the relative stretch of the fibre is

\[\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = \frac{2\pi(r + u_{\mathrm{r}}) - 2\pi r}{2\pi r} = \frac{u_{\mathrm{r}}}{r} . \tag{15.44}\]

This is not a derivative but a ratio: we divide the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) by the radius \(r\). In the tube of chapter 11 the inner surface has \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = 16{,}87\) µm at \(r = 40\) mm, so \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = 4{,}22 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and both sides of equation (15.44) give the same number (num-09.out, part 2). The figure is therefore exaggerated about 600 times.

The same term follows from corollary 11.21 of chapter 11 if we insert \(u_\theta = 0\) and a field without dependence on \(\theta\). The next lemma collects the strains, stresses and energy of an axisymmetric state.

Lemma 15.60 Strains, stresses and energy of an axisymmetric state (deformacije, napetosti in energija osnosimetričnega stanja)

Let \(\vek u\) be an axisymmetric state (definition 15.59) in an isotropic linearly elastic material with Lamé constants \(\lambda\), \(\mu\) (definition 3.10). Let

\[\vek\varepsilon = \begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} \\ \varepsilon_{\theta\theta} \\ \gamma_{\mathrm{rz}} \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \vek\sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{rz}} \end{bmatrix}\]

be the columns of local components with the engineering shear strain \(\gamma_{\mathrm{rz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rz}}\) (as in definition 3.18). Then:

  1. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \varepsilon_{\theta \mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \sigma_{\theta \mathrm{z}} = 0\) and
    \[\vek\varepsilon = \begin{bmatrix} \partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r \\ \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z \\ u_{\mathrm{r}}/r \\ \partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial r \end{bmatrix} . \tag{15.45}\]
  2. \(\vek\sigma = \mat C\,\vek\varepsilon\) with the matrix
    \[\mat C = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda + 2\mu & \lambda & \lambda & 0 \\ \lambda & \lambda + 2\mu & \lambda & 0 \\ \lambda & \lambda & \lambda + 2\mu & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \mu \end{bmatrix} . \tag{15.46}\]
  3. The strain energy density is \(\tfrac12\,\vek\sigma^\T\vek\varepsilon = \tfrac12\,\vek\varepsilon^\T\mat C\,\vek\varepsilon\).
Idea

Corollary 11.21 gives all six strains in cylindrical coordinates. When we insert \(u_\theta = 0\) and \(\partial/\partial\theta = 0\), four remain. Hooke's law in local axes is the same as in Cartesian ones, so the matrix \(\mat C\) is only a way of writing four of its equations.

Proof
  1. In equations (11.26) (corollary 11.21) we have \(u_\theta = 0\) and every derivative with respect to \(\theta\) is zero, because \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) do not depend on \(\theta\). What remains is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = u_{\mathrm{r}}/r\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial r)\), and the other two components are zero. The shear strain is \(\gamma_{\mathrm{rz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rz}}\).
  2. Hooke's law in local axes (corollary 11.26, equations (11.31)) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \lambda\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \varepsilon_{\theta\theta}) + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}}\), the same for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) with the roles of the strains exchanged, and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\), \(\sigma_{\theta \mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rz}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rz}} = \mu\,\gamma_{\mathrm{rz}}\). These are the rows of the equation \(\vek\sigma = \mat C\,\vek\varepsilon\).
  3. The energy density is \(\tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{ij}}\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 4.85). The term \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rz}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rz}}\) occurs twice (for \(rz\) and \(zr\)), so the sum is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta}\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{rz}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rz}} = \vek\sigma^\T\vek\varepsilon\) with \(\gamma_{\mathrm{rz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rz}}\). The last form follows from step 2. The sum \(\sum\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the trace of the matrix product \(\ten\sigma\ten\varepsilon\), and this does not change under an orthogonal change of axes, so we may write it in local components.

Source: ONATE1 (7.2)-(7.7) (PDF p. 250-251), COOK (14.1-5) (PDF p. 524) and (14.1-4) (PDF p. 523). ONATE1 writes the matrix \(\mat D\), we write \(\mat C\) as in section 15.4.

For steel \(\lambda = 113{,}08\) GPa, \(\mu = 75{,}38\) GPa and \(\lambda + 2\mu = 263{,}85\) GPa, which are the numbers of the matrix (15.46). The order of the components is as in the plane elements (first \(rr\) and \(zz\)), with \(\theta\theta\) added in between and the shear last. The symbols meet other meanings here: \(\mat B\) is the strain matrix (bold), not the constant \(B\) of Lamé's tube, \(J\) is the determinant of the Jacobian matrix of the element map, not the \(J = r\) of cylindrical coordinates, and \(\mat C\) is here the \(4 \times 4\) matrix that remains of the \(6 \times 6\) matrix \(\mat C\) of chapter 3 when we drop the two zero shears. We do not give the area a letter, because we write the integral over the set \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\).

The element has four nodes like the plane Q4 (section 15.5), only what we integrate changes.

Definition 15.61 Axisymmetric element (osnosimetrični element)

Let \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the section of a ring, a curved quadrilateral with nodes \((r_{\mathrm{i}}, z_{\mathrm{i}})\) for \(i = 1, \dots, 4\), that is the image of the square \([-1, 1]^2\) under an isoparametric map (definition 15.30) with shape functions \(N_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi, \eta) = \tfrac14(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi)(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)\) (equation (15.22)), \(r = \sum N_{\mathrm{i}} r_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(z = \sum N_{\mathrm{i}} z_{\mathrm{i}}\), and let \(J > 0\) at every point of the square (theorem 15.32). An axisymmetric element (osnosimetrični element) is the ring made by turning \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\) about the axis \(z\), with the displacement fields

\[u_{\mathrm{r}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^4 N_{\mathrm{i}}\,u_{\mathrm{ri}} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^4 N_{\mathrm{i}}\,u_{\mathrm{zi}} , \tag{15.47}\]

and the column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (u_{\mathrm{r}1}, u_{\mathrm{z}1}, \dots, u_{\mathrm{r}4}, u_{\mathrm{z}4})^\T\) of eight numbers. The number \(u_{\mathrm{ri}}\) is the radial and \(u_{\mathrm{zi}}\) the axial displacement of all points of the circle of node \(i\).

Source: ONATE1 §7.3 (PDF p. 254-255), COOK §14.2 (PDF p. 524), who describe the element as a torus with nodal circles. The definition follows the plane one, see chapter 7 for the two-node element.

Every ring is thus a two-dimensional element, but with a different integral. A plane element has a thickness \(t\), and here we must take into account that a solid of revolution weighs more the farther it is from the axis. Take \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\) between \(r = 40\) mm and \(50\) mm and \(z = 0\) and \(10\) mm, area \(100\) mm². The volume of its ring is \(\pi(50^2 - 40^2)\cdot 10 = 28\,274\) mm³. The same section between \(90\) mm and \(100\) mm gives \(\pi(100^2 - 90^2)\cdot 10 = 59\,690\) mm³, so \(2{,}11\) times as much. The ratio is \((100^2 - 90^2)/(50^2 - 40^2) = (190 \cdot 10)/(90 \cdot 10) = 95/45\), which is the ratio of the mean radii of the two sections, \(95\) and \(45\) mm. With the same width \(10\) mm the ring is thus as many times larger as its section is farther from the axis. Every quantity of the ring must therefore carry the weight \(r\), and the turn through the full angle gives another \(2\pi\).

Lemma 15.62 Stiffness and forces of an axisymmetric element (togost in sile osnosimetričnega elementa)

Let the element \(e\) be an axisymmetric element (definition 15.61) with the matrix \(\mat C\) of lemma 15.60 and \(\vek\varepsilon = \mat B\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), where the matrix \(\mat B\) of size \(4 \times 8\) has for each node \(i\) the columns \((2i - 1, 2i)\)

\[\mat B_{\mathrm{i}} = \begin{bmatrix} \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial r & 0 \\ 0 & \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial z \\ N_{\mathrm{i}}/r & 0 \\ \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial z & \partial N_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial r \end{bmatrix} , \tag{15.48}\]

and the derivatives with respect to \(r\) and \(z\) come from the inverse Jacobian matrix of the element map. Then:

  1. The strain energy of the ring is \(\tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the stiffness matrix (definition 7.4)
    \[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{e}}\mat B^\T\mat C\,\mat B\;2\pi r\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\!\int_{-1}^{1}\mat B^\T\mat C\,\mat B\;r\,J\,\mathrm{d}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\eta . \tag{15.49}\]
  2. The consistent forces (definition 7.7) are, for a body force \((b_{\mathrm{r}}, b_{\mathrm{z}})\), for a traction \((t_{\mathrm{r}}, t_{\mathrm{z}})\) on the surface that is the ring of an arc \(\Gamma \subset \partial\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\), and for an initial strain \(\vek\varepsilon_0\) (definition 7.48),
    \[\vek f_{\mathrm{e}} = \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{e}}\mat N^\T\vek b\;2\pi r\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\Gamma}\mat N^\T\vek t\;2\pi r\,\mathrm{d}s + \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{e}}\mat B^\T\mat C\,\vek\varepsilon_0\;2\pi r\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{15.50}\]
    where \(\mat N\) is the \(2 \times 8\) matrix with the entries \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) on the diagonals of its blocks. For a temperature change \(\Delta T\) we have \(\vek\varepsilon_0 = \alpha\,\Delta T\,(1, 1, 1, 0)^\T\) (theorem 3.15).
  3. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\) exactly when all \(u_{\mathrm{ri}} = 0\) and all \(u_{\mathrm{zi}}\) are equal. The only rigid motion of an axisymmetric element is the axial translation.
Idea

The volume is an integral over a set (definition 4.30), cylindrical coordinates are a change of variables with \(J = r\), and the integrand does not depend on \(\theta\), so Fubini's theorem gives the factor \(2\pi\). The rest is the same as for a plane element: we write the energy in nodal displacements.

Proof
  1. The ring is the image of the set \(D_{\mathrm{e}} = \Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\times(\theta_0, \theta_0 + 2\pi)\) (definition 15.59) and we cut the body by the surface at \(\theta_0\) as in theorem 11.27 (definition 4.21). By lemma 15.60 the function \(g = \tfrac12\,\vek\varepsilon^\T\mat C\,\vek\varepsilon\) is the energy per unit volume and depends on \((r, z)\) only. By theorem 4.59 with \(J = r\) (lemma 11.15) and Fubini's theorem (theorem 4.9),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{e}} g\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{e}}\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_0 + 2\pi} g(r, z)\,r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\pi\int_{\Omega_\mathrm{e}} g\,r\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
  2. By equation (15.47) and lemma 15.60, \(\vek\varepsilon = \mat B\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\): the first two rows are the derivatives \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) of the sums \(\sum N_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{ri}}\), the third is \(\sum N_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{ri}}/r\) and the fourth is the sum of derivatives. Inserting into step 1 gives \(\tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\big(\int\mat B^\T\mat C\,\mat B\,2\pi r\,\mathrm{d}A\big)\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), which is the first part of equation (15.49). The second part is the change of variables \((\xi, \eta) \mapsto (r, z)\) with determinant \(J\) (theorem 4.59).
  3. The work of the body force and the initial strain on a virtual field \(\vek w = \mat N\,\vek c\) is an integral over the ring, which by step 1 gives the same factor \(2\pi r\) in the integral over \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\). For a traction on the surface that is the ring of the arc \(\Gamma\) the work is an integral over the surface of revolution: each point of the arc at radius \(r\) carries a circle of length \(2\pi r\), so the integral over the surface equals the integral over the arc with the weight \(2\pi r\). For a line load \(q\) along a circle of radius \(r\) this is the force \(2\pi r q\) (COOK, PDF p. 526). This gives equation (15.50).
  4. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric, because \(\mat C\) is symmetric. For every \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) we have \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = 2\pi\int\vek\varepsilon^\T\mat C\,\vek\varepsilon\,r\,\mathrm{d}A \ge 0\), since \(\mat C\) is positive definite (theorem 3.48, \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\)). Equality holds exactly when \(\vek\varepsilon = \vek 0\) everywhere on \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\). Here \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\) holds exactly when \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\): the first gives the second, and if the second holds, the function \(\vek x \mapsto \vek x^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek x \ge 0\) has its smallest value at the point \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), so its gradient \(2\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) is zero there. The third row gives \(\sum N_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{ri}} = 0\), so all \(u_{\mathrm{ri}} = 0\), because the \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) are linearly independent. Then \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = 0\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial r = 0\), so \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) is constant on the connected set \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = c\). Since \(\sum N_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) (lemma 15.29, point 2), we get \(\sum N_{\mathrm{i}}\,(u_{\mathrm{zi}} - c) = 0\) and all \(u_{\mathrm{zi}}\) are equal to \(c\). A field with all \(u_{\mathrm{ri}} = 0\) and equal \(u_{\mathrm{zi}}\) has \(\vek\varepsilon = \vek 0\) by equation (15.45), so it is in the kernel.

Source: ONATE1 (7.13)-(7.16) and (7.25)-(7.29) (PDF p. 253-258), COOK (14.2-2) (PDF p. 524-525) and "\(r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\) instead of thickness" (PDF p. 525). The proof of the third point (the kernel) is not from the sources.

The integrand in equation (15.49) contains \(N_{\mathrm{i}}/r\) and is therefore not a polynomial. The \(2 \times 2\) Gauss rule (section 15.6) is used on it all the same. For \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\) of figure 15.33 the rule gives the volume of the ring \(V = 28\,274{,}33\) mm³, which is the exact value, because \(r J\) is linear in \(\xi\) for a rectangle. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) of this element has one zero eigenvalue of eight, and a plane element of the same shape has three (num-09.out): a plane element has three rigid motions in the plane, an axisymmetric one only the axial translation.

The reason is the circumferential strain of figure 15.34. Turn the section \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\) through the small angle \(10^{-3}\) about the origin of coordinates: in the plane this is a rigid motion with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rz}} = 0\), but at the point \(r = 45\) mm, \(z = 5\) mm the field \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -10^{-3}\,z\) has the circumferential strain \(u_{\mathrm{r}}/r = -1{,}11 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and for the ring this is not a rigid motion. COOK (PDF p. 525) calls this ring rolling: a plane element therefore could not carry a moment, an axisymmetric one can. For the system of equations it follows that it is enough to fix \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) of one circle of nodes (COOK, PDF p. 526).

One more peculiarity is the edge where \(r = 0\).

The element starts at the axis, and the nodes on the axis are circles of radius zero. If one of them moves radially by \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\), the edge of the element leaves the axis, and when we turn this, a hole of radius \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) appears in a body that was solid. COOK (PDF p. 526) writes that the hole doubles the circumferential stress at \(r = 0\), and that the radial displacement of all nodes on the axis must be suppressed. Our symmetry says the same: a point on the axis stays in place when turned about the axis, and its displacement must by axial symmetry be unchanged, so parallel to the axis.

Lemma 15.63 Points on the axis (točke na osi)

Let \(\vek u\) be an axisymmetric state (figure 15.35) whose \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuously differentiable also at \(r = 0\), and let the displacement field be continuous across the axis. Then:

  1. \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(0, z) = 0\).
  2. \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta}(0, z) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}}(0, z)\) as a limit, and \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta}\) need not be computed as \(0/0\).
Proof
  1. The displacement of a point in Cartesian axes is \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{r}}\cos\theta,\ u_{\mathrm{r}}\sin\theta,\ u_{\mathrm{z}})\) (equation (15.43) and lemma 11.15). The point \((0, 0, z)\) on the axis is the limit of points at every angle \(\theta\) and the field is continuous, so the displacement as \(r \to 0\) is the same for all \(\theta\). For \(\theta = 0\) the first component is \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(0, z)\), for \(\theta = \pi\) it is \(-u_{\mathrm{r}}(0, z)\), hence \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(0, z) = 0\).
  2. By step 1, \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = u_{\mathrm{r}}(r, z)/r = \big(u_{\mathrm{r}}(r, z) - u_{\mathrm{r}}(0, z)\big)/r\), which is the difference quotient of the function \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) in \(r\) at the point \(r = 0\) with the step \(r\). As \(r \to 0\) it tends to the derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r(0, z) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}}(0, z)\), because \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) is differentiable.

Source: COOK (PDF p. 525-526), ONATE1 (PDF p. 256), who also mention that there is no Gauss point at \(r = 0\). The proof is ours.

We test both points on a computation for the element of figure 15.35. The Gauss points of the element between \(r = 0\) and \(15\) mm in the \(2 \times 2\) rule lie at \(r = 3{,}17\) mm at the least, so \(N_{\mathrm{i}}/r\) is nowhere \(0/0\) (COOK, PDF p. 525). With \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) fixed on the axis, a solid cylinder of radius \(b = 60\) mm under an outer pressure \(p = 30\) MPa and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) at both ends (four Q4 across the radius) gives the edge displacement \(-4{,}7755\) µm, which is the exact value \(-(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)\,p\,b/E\), and without the fixing the nodes on the axis stay at \(0{,}0000\) µm. It is the same with another load, an axial pressure of \(30\) MPa on the upper end of the cylinder, which is supported at the lower end in the direction \(z\) only, with a free side (edge displacement \(\nu\,p\,b/E = 2{,}7551\) µm). These two tests say nothing about the fixing. In both the exact field is linear, \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) proportional to \(r\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) to \(z\), so it lies in the Q4 family and the mesh hits it with or without the fixing of the axis (theorem 6.34, point 1: in the family the energy is smallest at the exact field if the family contains it), and the exact field has \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) on the axis.

A real test is a load for which the exact field is not linear. Take the same cylinder with a radial body force \(b_{\mathrm{r}} = k\,r\) that grows with the radius, with \(k = 7{,}8 \cdot 10^9\) N/m⁴ (this force per unit volume acts on steel of density \(7800\) kg/m³ in a cylinder turning at the angular velocity \(1000\) 1/s), with a free side and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) at both ends. The edge displacement with four, eight and sixteen Q4 is the same with or without the fixing of the axis, \(1{,}1175\) µm. This is the exact value for every mesh. The field \(\vek w\) with \(w_{\mathrm{r}} = r\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) lies in the Q4 family, and for every field \(\vek v\) with \(v_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) we have \(\vek\varepsilon(\vek w)^\T\mat C\,\vek\varepsilon(\vek v)\,r = (2\lambda + 2\mu)\,\partial(r\,v_{\mathrm{r}})/\partial r\). The integral of this expression over the section, times \(2\pi\), is the bilinear form \(B(\vek v, \vek w)\) of lemma 6.36 and therefore depends only on \(v_{\mathrm{r}}\) at the edge \(r = b\) (09-check2.out). By this lemma it is zero for \(\vek v = \vek u - \vek u_{\mathrm{h}}\), where \(\vek u_{\mathrm{h}}\) is the finite element solution, so the exact solution and \(\vek u_{\mathrm{h}}\) have the same edge displacement, since neither depends on \(z\). The displacements of the inner nodes are not exact: the node at \(r = 15\) mm is off by \(2\,\%\) with four elements. But the unfixed nodes on the axis do not stay at zero: they get \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}0053\) µm, \(0{,}0007\) µm and \(0{,}0001\) µm, which for four elements is \(0{,}5\,\%\) of the edge displacement (09-check.out, part 3). Without the fixing there is thus a small hole of figure 15.35 on the axis, which closes as the mesh gets finer. The fixing closes it at once and costs nothing, so we keep it.

The question remains whether the solution by axisymmetric elements keeps the theorems of chapter 6. The field \(\vek u_{\mathrm{h}} = u_{\mathrm{r}}\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} + u_{\mathrm{z}}\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) of equation (15.47), assembled from elements, has in Cartesian components \((u_{\mathrm{r}}\cos\theta, u_{\mathrm{r}}\sin\theta, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) continuous values everywhere, also on the axis, if \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) there (lemma 15.63). On each ring it is continuously differentiable up to the boundary. Definition 15.13, however, needs a mesh in the sense of definition 15.12, and a whole ring is not a curved box: its faces at \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_0 + 2\pi\) coincide, so it shares a face with itself. We therefore cut every ring in thought into three sectors of \(120^\circ\), at the same angles \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\) for all rings. A sector is the image of the cube \([-1, 1]^3\) under the map \((\xi, \zeta, \eta) \mapsto (r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta,\ z)\), where \(r(\xi, \eta)\) and \(z(\xi, \eta)\) are the map of the element and \(\theta = \theta_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\pi}{3}(1 + \zeta)\). Its Jacobian determinant is \(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\,r\,J\), so it is positive if \(r > 0\) on the whole of \(\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\). Then the sector is a curved box (definition 4.65, for the section theorem 15.32). Neighbouring sectors share a whole face, so the sectors form a mesh and the field is a piecewise smooth field (definition 15.13). An element that touches the axis, as in the solid cylinder above and the sphere below, is not covered by this: on the axis \(r = 0\), the determinant is zero there and the sector is not a curved box. For such meshes the theorems of this chapter do not cover the following claim and this book does not prove it, the test with the sphere below only checks it on numbers.

For meshes that do not reach the axis the following holds. The space of fields assembled over the rings of such a mesh is a finite-dimensional subspace of the piecewise smooth fields of the body, so theorem 6.34 and theorem 6.39 hold as for the bar: the finite element solution minimizes the potential energy (theorem 4.91) among these fields and is the best approximation of the exact solution in the energy norm within them (corollary 15.16). The theorems do not need the exact solution to be axisymmetric. The ring fields, however, are all axisymmetric, so we use them only when the exact solution is axisymmetric too. Under an axisymmetric load and supports this follows from the argument at the start of the section, as for Lamé.

We test this on the first examples of chapter 11.

Example 15.64 Tube and sphere with axisymmetric elements (cev in krogla z osnosimetričnimi elementi)

The tube \(40\) to \(60\) mm with an inner pressure \(p = 30\) MPa and plane strain (theorem 11.27 with \(S = 2\nu A\), that is \(\varepsilon_0 = 0\)) has at the inner radius \(a = 40\) mm the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(a) = 16{,}873\) µm. We make it as a strip of the section \((r, z)\) of height \(H = 10\) mm with \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) at both ends. The pressure \(p\) on the inner surface is the force \(p\,2\pi a\,H\) on the ring, which by equation (15.50) with the functions \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) divides into halves on the two nodes of the surface. In the strip \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) everywhere because of the supports.

We mesh the thick spherical shell \(40\) to \(60\) mm with the same inner pressure (theorem 11.28) differently. By axial symmetry and symmetry about the plane \(z = 0\) a quarter of the section is enough, with \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) on the axis (lemma 15.63) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) at \(z = 0\). We justify the second condition as we justified axisymmetry at the start of the section. The mirror image of the solution in the plane \(z = 0\) solves the same problem, because the sphere and the pressure are symmetric about this plane. By theorem 11.4 it differs from the solution by a rigid motion at most, and the only rigid motion of the form (15.43) is an axial translation by some length \(c\) (the argument is the one of point 3 of lemma 15.62: a rigid motion has no strain, so \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = u_{\mathrm{r}}/r = 0\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) is constant). The reflection changes the sign of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), so \(-u_{\mathrm{z}}(r, 0) = u_{\mathrm{z}}(r, 0) + c\), hence \(u_{\mathrm{z}}(r, 0) = -c/2\) at all \(r\). We choose the rigid motion of the sphere, which has no supports, so that this is zero. Chapter 19 treats symmetry in general.

The ratio of \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(a)\) for the meshes of figure 15.36 and the exact values:

elements unknowns \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(a)\) / Lamé error
tube, 2 Q4 across the wall 6 \(0{,}98929\) \(1{,}07 \cdot 10^{-2}\)
tube, 4 Q4 10 \(0{,}99724\) \(2{,}76 \cdot 10^{-3}\)
tube, 8 Q4 18 \(0{,}99930\) \(6{,}97 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
tube, 1, 2, 4 Q8 \(0{,}99904\), \(0{,}99993\), \(1{,}00000\)
sphere, Q4 \(2 \times 4\) 24 \(0{,}95222\) \(4{,}8 \cdot 10^{-2}\)
sphere, Q4 \(4 \times 8\) 80 \(0{,}98778\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-2}\)
sphere, Q8 \(1 \times 2\) 20 \(0{,}99729\) \(2{,}7 \cdot 10^{-3}\)
sphere, Q8 \(2 \times 4\) 64 \(0{,}99980\) \(2 \cdot 10^{-4}\)

The exact \(u_{\mathrm{R}}(a)\) of the sphere (figure 15.36) is \(6{,}6864\) µm (theorem 11.28). For the tube the error falls \(3{,}87\) times when the step is halved and then \(3{,}97\) times, so about four times. This is how an error proportional to \(h^2\) behaves, where \(h\) is the mesh step: half the step gives a quarter of the error. For the hanging bar in chapter 7 the gap at the middle of an element between the parabola of the true field and the line of the element was proportional to \(h^2\). For the axisymmetric element we have not proved this order, the numbers only show it. For the sphere the error is larger at the same number of unknowns. The elements Q4 and Q8 differ in two things: Q4 has straight edges, chords that lie inside the arcs by at most \(R(1 - \cos 11{,}25^\circ) = 0{,}77\) mm at \(R = 40\) mm, and its field is bilinear, while Q8 has parabolic edges and a field of higher degree. We did not separate which difference contributes more.

Source: The numbers are our computations: mkk.out part G (tube and sphere, full code) and num-09.out part 3 (tube with a separate computation, same values). Lamé: chapter 11.

The tube needed only a pressure. To see that the elements also carry a temperature load, we take the tube of chapter 14.

Example 15.65 Heated tube (ogrevana cev)

The tube \(40\) to \(60\) mm is heated so that the inner surface is \(100\) K above the outer one, and the strip has \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) at both ends (plane strain). First we solve the conduction with the same Q4 elements: the conduction matrix has the factor \(2\pi r\) of lemma 15.62 (the justification and the closed solution \(T(r)\) are in chapter 14). Then with the obtained nodal \(T\) we compute the initial strain \(\vek\varepsilon_0 = \alpha\,T\,(1, 1, 1, 0)^\T\) and the forces \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\) by equation (15.50) with \(\alpha = 15 \cdot 10^{-6}\) 1/K. The circumferential stress at the centre of an element is \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) from row 3 of the equation \(\vek\sigma = \mat C\,(\vek\varepsilon - \vek\varepsilon_0)\) (theorem 3.15). On the axes are the radius and the circumferential stress. The exact curve is the thermal Lamé solution, the values from the mesh are the stresses of 16 Q4 elements across the wall.

The values at the wall are the points \(-238{,}08\) MPa and \(181{,}92\) MPa (chapter 14), and the values from the mesh are at the element centres, so not at the wall. The element nearest the inner wall gives \(-218{,}65\) MPa at \(r = 40{,}625\) mm, and the exact value at this radius is \(-218{,}50\) MPa. All 16 values lie within \(0{,}14\) MPa of the curve. For coarse meshes the difference is larger:

elements across the wall \(r\) of the first centre (mm) \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) mesh (MPa) exact at this \(r\) (MPa)
2 \(45{,}00\) \(-103{,}49\) \(-97{,}74\)
4 \(42{,}50\) \(-165{,}36\) \(-163{,}51\)
8 \(41{,}25\) \(-200{,}10\) \(-199{,}58\)
16 \(40{,}625\) \(-218{,}65\) \(-218{,}50\)

The value at the wall itself (figure 15.37) needs the stresses to be extended from the centres to the wall, which we do not do here. The largest difference \(0{,}14\) MPa for 16 elements is \(0{,}06\,\%\) of the stress \(238{,}08\) MPa.

Source: Our computations: mkk.out part J (table, full code) and num-09.out part 6 (16 elements, all values).

The section showed that a plane mesh of the section is enough for a solid of revolution under an axisymmetric load, if we give the elements the circumferential strain \(u_{\mathrm{r}}/r\) and the weight \(2\pi r\) and if we hold the displacements on the axis. What remains are loads that are not axisymmetric: ONATE1 (PDF p. 248) expands them in a Fourier series in \(\theta\) and solves each term with a two-dimensional mesh, and COOK (PDF p. 522) treats this later in the same chapter, but the book does not. Thin solids of revolution (shells) are treated in chapter 22, and the three-dimensional elements that solve everything else in section 15.10.

15.10 Solid elements: the tetrahedron and the brick

A vessel for compressed gas has the shape of a thick spherical shell, of the kind we solved exactly in chapter 11 (theorem 11.28): steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), inner radius \(a = 40\) mm, outer radius \(b = 60\) mm and pressure \(p = 30\) MPa on the inner surface. The exact solution has a single displacement \(u_{\mathrm{R}}(a) = 6{,}6864\ \mu\)m on the inner surface. But what about a body for which there is no solution, for example a bearing housing or an engine head? There we must cut the body into elements, not in a plane but in space. In sections 15.1 to 15.9 we learned all the ingredients in the plane: coordinates with areas, the element with a linear field, the isoparametric map, the Gauss rules, the patch test and locking. Now we carry them into space and test them on exactly this shell, to see how close we come to the Lamé solution.

In the plane the basic pieces were the triangle and the quadrilateral. In space two other pieces replace them. The first is the tetrahedron (tetraeder, from the Greek words for four and face: it has four triangular faces), which in space is what the triangle is in the plane: with it we can fill every body with flat faces. The second is the brick (opeka, hexahedron, "six-face", six quadrilateral faces), the image of a cube, which the isoparametric map bends and stretches, just as it does a square in the plane. Let us begin with the tetrahedron.

15.10.1 Volume coordinates and the tetrahedron

For the triangle we fixed a point by ratios of areas (definition 15.3). We do the same with volumes. Imagine a tetrahedron with nodes \(\vek x_1, \dots, \vek x_4\) and a point \(P\) in it (figure 15.38, left). The point \(P\) cuts the tetrahedron, with segments to the four nodes, into four smaller tetrahedra. The one opposite node \(1\) has volume \(V_1\), and comparing it with the volume \(V\) of the whole tetrahedron gives a number between \(0\) and \(1\) that tells how close to node \(1\) the point \(P\) lies. There are four such numbers and their sum is \(1\), because the four pieces add up to the whole. Before we name them we must prove that this is well defined, that is, that the volume \(V\) of the tetrahedron is really different from zero and that the numbers really determine the point.

Definition 15.66 Volume coordinates (prostorninske koordinate)

Let \(\vek x_1, \vek x_2, \vek x_3, \vek x_4\) be four points in space that do not lie in one plane, that is \(\det\mat A \ne 0\) for the matrix \(\mat A\) with columns \(\vek a = \vek x_2 - \vek x_1\), \(\vek b = \vek x_3 - \vek x_1\), \(\vek c = \vek x_4 - \vek x_1\). The volume coordinates (prostorninske koordinate) of a point \(\vek x\) are the numbers \(L_1, L_2, L_3, L_4\) for which

\[L_1 + L_2 + L_3 + L_4 = 1 , \qquad L_1\vek x_1 + L_2\vek x_2 + L_3\vek x_3 + L_4\vek x_4 = \vek x . \tag{15.51}\]

The tetrahedron (tetraeder) with nodes \(\vek x_1, \dots, \vek x_4\) is the set of points in which all four coordinates are nonnegative, \(L_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\). The coordinate \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\) is always written with an index, because \(L\) elsewhere in the book is a length. The volume of the tetrahedron is \(V = |\det\mat A|/6\).

Source: ONATE1 §8.6, equations (8.57) to (8.59) (PDF p. 300), where the \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\) are quotients of volumes. The form above with the equations (15.51) is mine, so that the coordinates exist also outside the tetrahedron.

We shall justify the name "volume" with the next lemma: the coordinate \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\) really is a ratio of volumes, as in the figure. The lemma also says that every point gets exactly one quadruple of numbers and that the coordinates are linear functions of the point.

Lemma 15.67 Properties of the volume coordinates (lastnosti prostorninskih koordinat)

Let \(\vek x_1, \dots, \vek x_4\) be as in definition 15.66. Then:

  1. For every point \(\vek x\) there is exactly one quadruple \((L_1, \dots, L_4)\) that satisfies the equations (15.51).
  2. Every coordinate is a polynomial of degree one in \(\vek x\), \(L_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) = c_{\mathrm{i}} + \vek g_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek x\), with vectors \(\vek g_2 = \vek b\times\vek c/\det\mat A\), \(\vek g_3 = \vek c\times\vek a/\det\mat A\), \(\vek g_4 = \vek a\times\vek b/\det\mat A\) and \(\vek g_1 = -\vek g_2 - \vek g_3 - \vek g_4\). The gradient of a coordinate is therefore a constant vector.
  3. \(L_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x_{\mathrm{j}}) = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and the coordinate \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\) is zero exactly in the plane of the face opposite node \(i\).
  4. For a point in the tetrahedron \(L_{\mathrm{i}} = V_{\mathrm{i}}/V\), where \(V_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the volume of the tetrahedron obtained when in \(\vek x_1, \dots, \vek x_4\) the node \(i\) is replaced by the point \(\vek x\).
  5. The tetrahedron has volume \(V = |\det\mat A|/6\), as the definition claims.
Proof

We must show that the system of equations (15.51) has a single solution, write it down and read off the volumes. The first equation is used to eliminate \(L_1\).

  1. From \(L_1 = 1 - L_2 - L_3 - L_4\) and the second equation (15.51) it follows that \(\vek x - \vek x_1 = L_2\vek a + L_3\vek b + L_4\vek c\), that is \(\mat A\,(L_2, L_3, L_4)^\T = \vek x - \vek x_1\).
  2. Since \(\det\mat A \ne 0\), by theorem 2.54 on the inverse matrix with the determinant, \(\mat A\) has an inverse with rows \(\vek b\times\vek c/\det\mat A\), \(\vek c\times\vek a/\det\mat A\), \(\vek a\times\vek b/\det\mat A\). So the solution is unique, \(L_2 = \vek g_2\cdot(\vek x - \vek x_1)\), \(L_3 = \vek g_3\cdot(\vek x - \vek x_1)\), \(L_4 = \vek g_4\cdot(\vek x - \vek x_1)\) and \(L_1 = 1 - L_2 - L_3 - L_4\). These are polynomials of degree one, with gradients \(\vek g_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\vek g_1 = -\vek g_2 - \vek g_3 - \vek g_4\). This proves points 1 and 2.
  3. At \(\vek x = \vek x_{\mathrm{j}}\) we have \(\vek x_{\mathrm{j}} - \vek x_1 = \vek a\), \(\vek b\) or \(\vek c\) (or \(\vek 0\)), so by point 4 of lemma 2.31 (\(\vek a\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = 0\)) the scalar products \(\vek g_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek a\) and so on equal \(\delta\), and \(\det\mat A = \vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)\). Thus \(L_2(\vek x_2) = \vek g_2\cdot\vek a = 1\), \(L_2(\vek x_3) = \vek g_2\cdot\vek b = 0\) and \(L_2(\vek x_4) = 0\), similarly for \(L_3\) and \(L_4\), and \(L_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x_1) = 0\) for \(i = 2, 3, 4\), so \(L_1(\vek x_1) = 1\). The equation \(L_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) is the equation of the plane through the three nodes that are not \(\vek x_{\mathrm{i}}\) (these are the nodes with \(L_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) by the first part and \(\vek g_{\mathrm{i}} \ne \vek 0\)).
  4. For \(i = 2\) insert into the volume of the tetrahedron \(\vek x_1, \vek x, \vek x_3, \vek x_4\) the columns \(\vek x - \vek x_1\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\): its determinant is \((\vek x - \vek x_1)\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c) = L_2\det\mat A\). By point 5, then, \(V_2 = |L_2|\,V\), and in the tetrahedron \(L_2 \ge 0\). For \(i = 3, 4\) the computation is the same. For \(i = 1\) we renumber the nodes: the definition does not depend on the numbering.
  5. Let \(T_0\) be the tetrahedron with nodes \((0,0,0)\), \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\), \((0,0,1)\). By definition 4.20 for a body between graphs its volume is \(\int_0^1\int_0^{1-\xi}\int_0^{1-\xi-\eta}1\,\mathrm{d}\zeta\,\mathrm{d}\eta\,\mathrm{d}\xi = \tfrac16\). The map \(\vek\xi \mapsto \vek x_1 + \mat A\vek\xi\) takes \(T_0\) onto the tetrahedron with coordinates \(L_2 = \xi\), \(L_3 = \eta\), \(L_4 = \zeta\) and \(L_1 = 1 - \xi - \eta - \zeta\), that is, onto the set \(L_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\). By theorem 4.58 on the volume under a linear map, the volume of the image is \(|\det\mat A|\cdot\tfrac16\).

Source: ONATE1 §8.6 (PDF pp. 300-302): the definition of the coordinates as ratios of volumes and \(\sum L_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\). The proof with a system of equations and with the theorem on the inverse matrix is not from the source.

Example 15.68 A steel tetrahedron (jeklen tetraeder)

Take the tetrahedron with nodes \((0, 0, 0)\), \((40, 0, 0)\), \((10, 30, 0)\) and \((10, 10, 30)\) mm. The base face \(1\,2\,3\) is a triangle of area \(600\) mm² (the area of a triangle was computed in section 15.1), the height to node \(4\) is \(30\) mm, so \(V = 600\cdot 30/3 = 6000\) mm³. The determinant is \(\det\mat A = 36\,000\) mm³, six times the volume, as point 5 of the lemma requires (SymPy and NumPy, num-10.out). The point \(P = (15, 10, 6)\) mm cuts the tetrahedron into pieces with \(V_1 = 1650\), \(V_2 = 1550\), \(V_3 = 1600\), \(V_4 = 1200\) mm³, which add up to \(6000\) mm³, and

\[L_1 = 0{,}275 , \quad L_2 = 0{,}2583 , \quad L_3 = 0{,}2667 , \quad L_4 = 0{,}2 ,\]

as given also by the solution of the system (15.51) (check \(\sum L_{\mathrm{i}}\vek x_{\mathrm{i}} = (15, 10, 6)\) mm). The point is near the centroid, so all four are near \(1/4\). The smallest is \(L_4\), because, measured by the height of the tetrahedron, \(P\) is nearest to the face \(1\,2\,3\) opposite node \(4\): it is only \(6\) of \(30\) mm above it, and \(L_4 = 6/30 = 0{,}2\).

The gradients of the coordinates (unit 1/mm) are by point 2 of lemma 15.67

\[\vek g_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}025 \\ -0{,}025 \\ -0{,}01667 \end{bmatrix} , \quad \vek g_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}025 \\ -0{,}00833 \\ -0{,}00556 \end{bmatrix} , \quad \vek g_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0{,}03333 \\ -0{,}01111 \end{bmatrix} , \quad \vek g_4 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0{,}03333 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

the sum is \(\vek 0\), since \(\sum L_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) is constant. For \(\vek g_4\) only the third component is different from zero, \(1/30\) mm⁻¹: \(L_4\) grows from \(0\) on the plane \(z = 0\) to \(1\) at the height \(30\) mm.

The name is justified. Now we make a finite element out of the tetrahedron, as we made one out of two nodes for the bar element (definition 7.1).

Definition 15.69 The four-node tetrahedron (tetraeder s štirimi vozlišči, T4)

The element T4 is a tetrahedron with nodes \(\vek x_1, \dots, \vek x_4\) (definition 15.66) and with three displacements \(u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}}\) at each node, in all \(12\) degrees of freedom, collected in a column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\). The shape functions (definition 7.2) are the volume coordinates, \(N_{\mathrm{i}} = L_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the field of displacements in the element is

\[\vek u(\vek x) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{4} L_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x)\,\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} . \tag{15.52}\]

The vector \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the displacement of node \(i\).

Source: ONATE1 §8.6 (PDF p. 301): for the four-node tetrahedron the volume coordinates coincide with the shape functions. COOK section 6.5 (PDF pp. 231-232) knows the same element as a special case of the isoparametric 3D element.

Two questions are the same as for the triangle. Can the field (15.52) show the simple states, for example a translation and a stretch, that we know? And do neighbouring elements agree on a common face, so that no crack appears in the body? The answer yes to both is given by the next lemma.

Lemma 15.70 The field of the T4 element (polje elementa T4)

Let \(\vek u\) be the field (15.52) on a T4 element.

  1. The field is affine, \(\vek u(\vek x) = \vek c + \mat W\vek x\), and the gradient \(\mat W\) is constant. Every affine field \(\vek c + \mat W\vek x\) is on the element equal to the field (15.52) with nodal values \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek c + \mat W\vek x_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  2. If two T4 elements have a common face with three nodes, their fields agree on the face, because there they depend only on the three common nodal values.
Proof

We must show that the field is a polynomial of degree one, that the affine fields are contained and that the value on a face is determined by three nodes.

  1. By point 2 of lemma 15.67 every \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\) is a polynomial of degree one, so the sum (15.52), a linear combination of them, is also a polynomial of degree one in \(\vek x\).
  2. Let \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek c + \mat W\vek x_{\mathrm{i}}\). Then \(\sum L_{\mathrm{i}}\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek c\sum L_{\mathrm{i}} + \mat W\sum L_{\mathrm{i}}\vek x_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek c + \mat W\vek x\) by the equations (15.51).
  3. On the face opposite node \(i\) we have \(L_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) (point 3 of lemma 15.67), so the field there is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}\ne \mathrm{i}}L_{\mathrm{j}}\vek u_{\mathrm{j}}\). The remaining three coordinates are on the plane of the face the area coordinates of the triangle (definition 15.3), determined by the three nodes and the point. Two elements that share these three nodes have on the face the same coordinates and the same nodal values, so the same field.

Source: The proof is not from the source. ONATE1 §8.6 (PDF pp. 300-301) gives the coordinates and the linear interpolation.

Point 2 of the lemma says that the field is continuous across a face, so the field on a mesh of tetrahedra is a piecewise smooth field (section 15.2): for T4 the theorems for the Ritz method hold, as proved in that section. The condition "three common nodes" is not small. If a node of one tetrahedron lies in the interior of a face of another, the two do not share it and the fields on the face are not determined by the same numbers, so in general they differ and a jump appears, as for the hanging node of triangles (section 15.1).

The tetrahedron has one more condition, which we already required in definition 15.66: the four nodes must not lie in a plane. Let us see what happens when we approach this limit. In example 15.68 we lower node \(4\) from the height \(30\) mm to \(h = 3\) mm. The gradient \(\vek g_4\) is then \((0, 0, 1/h) = (0, 0, 0{,}3333)\) mm⁻¹, ten times larger, and as \(h \to 0\) it grows beyond all bounds, because \(L_4\) rises from \(0\) to \(1\) over an ever shorter height. The third components of the other three gradients are \(-1/(2h)\), \(-1/(6h)\) and \(-1/(3h)\) (SymPy) and grow in the same way. The stiffness matrix, which we derive below, is the volume \(V = 200\,h\) mm³ times a product of two matrices made of the gradients, so its entries grow like \(1/h\): a very flat tetrahedron is useless. At \(h = 0\) we have \(\det\mat A = 0\) and the coordinates do not exist.

Heat conduction on the tetrahedron

First we look at a scalar field, the temperature, as for the triangle (section 15.3): one unknown per node, no \(3 \times 3\) blocks. The functional of the heat problem is \(\frac12\int k\,|\nabla T|^2\,\mathrm{d}V\) plus the load terms (chapter 14), \(k\) is the thermal conductivity. What do we get if \(T\) is the field (15.52) with nodal temperatures \(T_{\mathrm{i}}\)?

Lemma 15.71 Conduction matrix of the tetrahedron (prevodnostna matrika tetraedra)

Let \(\mat G\) be the \(3 \times 4\) matrix with columns \(\vek g_1, \dots, \vek g_4\) from lemma 15.67, \(k\) the thermal conductivity and \(V\) the volume of the element. The temperature \(T = \sum L_{\mathrm{i}} T_{\mathrm{i}}\) has in the element a constant gradient \(\nabla T = \mat G\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\) and

\[\frac12\int_{\text{element}} k\,|\nabla T|^2\,\mathrm{d}V = \frac12\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}} , \qquad \mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = k\,V\,\mat G^\T\mat G . \tag{15.53}\]

The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, the sum of every row is zero, and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek T = \vek 0\) exactly for constant temperatures \(T_{\mathrm{i}} = \text{const}\).

Proof

We must show that the integral can be computed as a product and that the matrix has the listed properties.

  1. By point 2 of lemma 15.67 \(\nabla L_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek g_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant, so \(\nabla T = \sum T_{\mathrm{i}}\vek g_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat G\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  2. The integrand \(k\,|\mat G\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}|^2\) is constant in the element, so its integral over a set of volume \(V\) equals the value times \(V\) (lemma 4.32, point 1): \(\tfrac12 k V\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat G^\T\mat G\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\). This is the equation (15.53).
  3. The matrix is symmetric, since \((\mat G^\T\mat G)^\T = \mat G^\T\mat G\). For arbitrary \(\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\), \(\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek T_{\mathrm{e}} = kV\,|\mat G\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}|^2 \ge 0\). So the matrix is positive semidefinite, and by lemma 7.16 \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek T_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\) exactly when \(\mat G\vek T_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\).
  4. The sum of the coordinates is \(1\), so \(\sum\vek g_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek 0\), that is \(\mat G(1, 1, 1, 1)^\T = \vek 0\). Hence \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek 1 = \vek 0\): the sum of every row is zero. Conversely, if \(\mat G\vek T_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\), the gradient of the field \(T\) is zero, and the field is affine (lemma 15.70), so constant.

Source: The form after ONATE1 §4.3 (PDF pp. 155-168) for the triangle, the same with three components of the gradient. COOK section 12.2 (PDF pp. 473-475). The proof is not from the source.

For the tetrahedron of example 15.68 at \(k = 1\) W/(mm K) the matrix (unit W/K) is

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \begin{bmatrix} 9{,}167 & -1{,}944 & -3{,}889 & -3{,}333 \\ -1{,}944 & 4{,}352 & -1{,}296 & -1{,}111 \\ -3{,}889 & -1{,}296 & 7{,}407 & -2{,}222 \\ -3{,}333 & -1{,}111 & -2{,}222 & 6{,}667 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

with eigenvalues \(0\), \(5{,}719\), \(9{,}193\) and \(12{,}681\) (num-10.out). One eigenvalue is zero, since the kernel of the matrix is a single direction, constant temperature. The field \(T = 20 + 0{,}5\,x - 0{,}2\,y + 0{,}1\,z\) has at the nodes the values \(20\), \(40\), \(19\) and \(26\), and \(\mat G\vek T_{\mathrm{e}} = (0{,}5, -0{,}2, 0{,}1)\) K/mm is exactly its gradient: the element shows every linear temperature distribution.

For the triangle the edges where the body gives heat to its surroundings are segments. For the tetrahedron they are faces, which have an area. For the convection terms we need integrals of the products \(L_{\mathrm{i}}L_{\mathrm{j}}\) over a face, which are given by the formula for area coordinates (lemma 15.9): \(\int L_{\mathrm{i}}L_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}A = A/12\) for \(i \ne j\) and \(\int L_{\mathrm{i}}^2\,\mathrm{d}A = A/6\), where \(A\) is the area of the face and \(i\) and \(j\) are nodes of that face (the coordinate of the fourth node is zero on the face). The convection matrix of each face is assembled from them, as given for the triangle in chapter 14. The spatial problem (AK 9) is thus the same as the planar one: the same element matrix \(kV\mat G^\T\mat G\), only the vectors \(\vek g_{\mathrm{i}}\) have three components, and the assembly by theorem 7.13 is the same.

Stiffness matrix of the tetrahedron

In elasticity the unknowns are three displacements at a node, and the strain is a symmetric tensor with six components. In Voigt notation (definition 3.18, order \(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(yz\), \(xz\), \(xy\) with engineering shear strains \(\gamma = 2\varepsilon\)) the small strain tensor (definition 1.115) is linear in the displacements: \(\{\varepsilon\} = \mat B\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\). For T4 the \(6 \times 12\) matrix \(\mat B\) has blocks with three columns each

\[\mat B_{\mathrm{i}} = \begin{bmatrix} g_{\mathrm{ix}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & g_{\mathrm{iy}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & g_{\mathrm{iz}} \\ 0 & g_{\mathrm{iz}} & g_{\mathrm{iy}} \\ g_{\mathrm{iz}} & 0 & g_{\mathrm{ix}} \\ g_{\mathrm{iy}} & g_{\mathrm{ix}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat B = \begin{bmatrix} \mat B_1 & \mat B_2 & \mat B_3 & \mat B_4 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{15.54}\]

where \(g_{\mathrm{ix}}, g_{\mathrm{iy}}, g_{\mathrm{iz}}\) are the components of the vector \(\vek g_{\mathrm{i}}\). Since the \(\vek g_{\mathrm{i}}\) are constant, \(\mat B\) is a constant matrix, and the strain in the element is constant: the element is the spatial relative of the constant-strain triangle (section 15.4).

The material matrix \(\mat C\) of an isotropic material in Voigt order (theorem 3.11, lemma 3.19) has the value \(\lambda + 2\mu\) on the diagonal of the upper \(3 \times 3\) block, \(\lambda\) off the diagonal and \(\mu\) in the remaining diagonal (ONATE1 writes this matrix \(\mat D\), we keep \(\mat C\) from chapter 3). For steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\) we have \(\lambda = 113{,}08\) GPa, \(\mu = 75{,}38\) GPa and \(\lambda + 2\mu = 263{,}85\) GPa.

Lemma 15.72 Stiffness matrix of the tetrahedron (togostna matrika tetraedra)

Let \(\mat C\) be the material matrix of an isotropic linearly elastic material with \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\), and \(V\) the volume of the T4 element. The strain energy of the element is \(\tfrac12\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) with

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = V\,\mat B^\T\mat C\,\mat B . \tag{15.55}\]

The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d = \vek 0\) exactly for six independent rigid motions \(\vek u = \vek a + \vek\omega\times\vek x\), at the nodes \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (\vek a + \vek\omega\times\vek x_{\mathrm{i}})_{\mathrm{i}}\) with arbitrary \(\vek a\) and \(\vek\omega\). Of the twelve columns of the matrix, \(12 - 6 = 6\) are independent.

Proof

We must show that the energy gives the written matrix, and then find the vectors for which the energy is zero.

  1. The strain energy density is \(\tfrac12\{\varepsilon\}^\T\mat C\{\varepsilon\}\) (definition 4.85) and for an isotropic material with the given constants it is positive for every nonzero strain (theorem 3.48). Since \(\{\varepsilon\} = \mat B\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) is constant, the energy of the element by lemma 4.32, point 1, equals \(\tfrac12 V\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat B^\T\mat C\mat B\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric, because \(\mat C\) is symmetric. For every \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = V\{\varepsilon\}^\T\mat C\{\varepsilon\} \ge 0\), and it is zero exactly when \(\{\varepsilon\} = \vek 0\) (point 1). By lemma 7.16 the kernel of \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the set of all \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(\mat B\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\).
  3. The field of the element is affine, \(\vek u = \vek c + \mat W\vek x\) (lemma 15.70) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) determines it uniquely, since the four nodes are not coplanar. The strain is the symmetric part \(\tfrac12(\mat W + \mat W^\T)\) of the matrix \(\mat W\) (definition 1.115), and is zero exactly for a skew-symmetric \(\mat W\). Such a \(\mat W\) has three independent numbers, and we write it as \(\mat W\vek x = \vek\omega\times\vek x\). The kernel is thus \(\{\vek c + \vek\omega\times\vek x\}\) with six parameters \(\vek c\) and \(\vek\omega\) and has dimension \(6\).

Source: ONATE1 §8.3 and §8.6 (PDF pp. 284-286, 300-306) and COOK section 6.5 (PDF pp. 231-232) for the form \(\mat B^\T\mat C\mat B\,V\). The proof about the kernel is not from the source.

For the tetrahedron of example 15.68 the \(12 \times 12\) matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) has exactly six eigenvalues that, compared with the largest (\(4{,}7\cdot 10^9\) N/m), are zero up to rounding (up to \(10^{-6}\) N/m), and the remaining six lie between \(9{,}9\cdot 10^8\) and \(4{,}7\cdot 10^9\) N/m. For three translations \(\vek a\) and three rotations \(\vek\omega\), \(\|\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d\|/(\|\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\|\,\|\vek d\|) \sim 10^{-17}\). For the affine field \(\vek u = \mat W\vek x\) with \(\mat W = 10^{-3}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\) and nodal displacements \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat W\vek x_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(\mat B\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) gives the strain \((1, -1, 2, 3, 1, 2)\cdot 10^{-3}\), as given directly by \(\tfrac12(\mat W + \mat W^\T)\) with \(\gamma = 2\varepsilon\), for example \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = W_{\mathrm{yz}} + W_{\mathrm{zy}} = (3 + 0)\cdot 10^{-3}\) (num-10.out).

Load on the tetrahedron

As for the bar (definition 7.7) we move the load to the nodes with the same requirement: the work stays the same. For T4 two integrals of the shape functions are needed.

Lemma 15.73 Consistent forces of the tetrahedron (konsistentne sile tetraedra)

Let a T4 element have volume \(V\).

  1. A constant body force \(\vek b\) (N/m³) gives every node the force \(\vek b\,V/4\).
  2. A constant surface force \(\vek t\) (N/m²) on a face of area \(A\) gives each of the three nodes of that face the force \(\vek t\,A/3\), and the fourth node zero.
Proof

We must show \(\int L_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}V = V/4\) and \(\int L_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A = A/3\).

  1. The consistent force is \(\vek f_{\mathrm{i}} = \int\vek b\,L_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}V\) (definition 7.7 in three dimensions). By theorem 4.59 on the change of variables with the affine map \(\vek\xi \mapsto \vek x_1 + \mat A\vek\xi\) from the proof of lemma 15.67 (point 5), \(\int L_2\,\mathrm{d}V = |\det\mat A|\int_{\mathrm{T}_0}\xi\,\mathrm{d}V = 6V\cdot\tfrac1{24} = V/4\), since \(\int_{\mathrm{T}_0}\xi = \tfrac1{24}\) (iterated integral, SymPy). The same for \(L_3\) and \(L_4\), and from \(L_1 = 1 - L_2 - L_3 - L_4\) it follows that \(\int L_1 = V - \tfrac34V = V/4\).
  2. On a face one coordinate is zero, the remaining three are the area coordinates of the face, and by lemma 15.9 with \(a = 1\), \(\int L_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 1!\cdot 2A/3! = A/3\).

Source: ONATE1 §8.3.5 (PDF pp. 286-288) for the notion of "equivalent nodal force", the formula follows from the computation above.

Our steel tetrahedron of density \(7850\) kg/m³ weighs \(\rho\,g\,V = 0{,}462\) N (\(V = 6\cdot 10^{-6}\) m³), and each of the four nodes receives \(0{,}1155\) N downwards. If a pressure of \(1\) MPa acts on the face \(1\,2\,3\), that is a force of \(600\) N on the area \(600\) mm², each of the nodes \(1\), \(2\), \(3\) receives \(200\) N. A point force acts directly on a node. An initial strain due to temperature (chapter 3, definition 3.13) gives the force \(V\mat B^\T\mat C\{\varepsilon_0\}\) with \(\{\varepsilon_0\} = \alpha\Delta T\,(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)^\T\), as for the bar (lemma 7.49) and in the plane (section 15.4).

15.10.2 The brick with eight nodes

The tetrahedron has constant strain, which in bending is too stiff, as we saw for the triangle and the cantilever. A better piece is the image of a cube. Let \([-1, 1]^3\) be a cube with natural coordinates \(\xi\), \(\eta\), \(\zeta\) (figure 15.39, left). Its nodes are numbered \(1\) to \(8\) and lie at the corners \((\xi_{\mathrm{i}}, \eta_{\mathrm{i}}, \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}) \in \{-1, 1\}^3\), the lower quadrilateral \(1\) to \(4\) at \(\zeta = -1\) and the upper \(5\) to \(8\) at \(\zeta = 1\). The axes are the directions of increasing coordinates. For each node we make a function that is \(1\) at it and \(0\) at the other seven: a product of three linear functions, one in each coordinate.

Definition 15.74 The eight-node brick (opeka z osmimi vozlišči, H8)

Let \(\vek x_1, \dots, \vek x_8\) be nodes numbered like the corners of the cube \([-1, 1]^3\). The shape functions (definition 7.2) are

\[N_{\mathrm{i}}(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = \tfrac18\,(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\xi)(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)(1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\zeta) , \qquad i = 1, \dots, 8 , \tag{15.56}\]

with \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}, \eta_{\mathrm{i}}, \zeta_{\mathrm{i}} \in \{-1, 1\}\) the coordinates of node \(i\) in the cube. The geometry and the displacement field follow the same recipe (isoparametric element, definition 15.30):

\[\Phi(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{8}N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek x_{\mathrm{i}} , \qquad \vek u = \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{8}N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} , \tag{15.57}\]

and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) has \(24\) numbers. The brick (hexahedron) is the image \(\Phi([-1, 1]^3)\) if \(\Phi\) is a curved box (definition 4.65).

Source: ONATE1 §8.4 (PDF pp. 288-289), COOK section 6.5 (PDF pp. 231-232), equation (6.5-2) for the Jacobian matrix.

The functions (15.56) have the same properties as for the quadrilateral (section 15.5), and the proof is the same in three coordinates. In short: \(N_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek\xi_{\mathrm{j}}) = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the sum of the functions is the product \(\tfrac12[(1 - \xi) + (1 + \xi)]\cdot\tfrac12[(1 - \eta) + (1 + \eta)]\cdot\tfrac12[(1 - \zeta) + (1 + \zeta)] = 1\), and therefore the field (15.57) contains every affine field on every brick (lemma 15.35). On the face \(\zeta = 1\) the four functions with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}} = -1\) are zero, so the map and the field there are determined by the four nodes of the face, and two bricks with a common face of four nodes agree on it. The condition that all four nodes are common is necessary here too.

For the quadrilateral the Jacobian determinant was linear and its sign could be seen already at the corners. Here it is not so.

Lemma 15.75 Jacobian determinant of the brick (Jacobijeva determinanta opeke)

Let \(J = \det\mat F_\Phi\) be the determinant of the matrix of derivatives \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial\xi_{\mathrm{j}}\) of the map (15.57).

  1. \(J\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(2\) in each of the coordinates \(\xi\), \(\eta\), \(\zeta\).
  2. If the nodes are the corners of a parallelepiped, numbered so that \(\det\mat A > 0\) for the matrix \(\mat A\) of the edges from node \(1\) (in the proof), \(J\) is constant, equal to \(V/8\), where \(V\) is the volume of the parallelepiped.
  3. If \(\Phi\) is a curved box, the volume of the brick is \(V = \int_{[-1,1]^3}J\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}\in\{1,2\}}w_{\mathrm{i}}w_{\mathrm{j}}w_{\mathrm{k}}\,J(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}, \xi_{\mathrm{j}}, \xi_{\mathrm{k}})\) with the Gauss rule of two points in each coordinate.
Proof

We must show the degree estimate, the value for a parallelepiped and the exactness of the rule.

  1. The column \(\partial\Phi/\partial\xi\) contains the functions \(\tfrac18\xi_{\mathrm{i}}(1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}}\eta)(1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\zeta)\), which are of degree \(0\) in \(\xi\) and \(1\) in \(\eta\) and \(\zeta\). Similarly the columns \(\partial\Phi/\partial\eta\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial\zeta\) are of degree \(0\) in their own coordinate and \(1\) in the other two. Every term of the expansion of the determinant (definition 2.50) is a product of one element from each column, so it is in \(\xi\) of degree at most \(0 + 1 + 1 = 2\), the same in \(\eta\) and \(\zeta\).
  2. For a parallelepiped \(\vek x_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek x_1 + \tfrac12[(1 + \xi_{\mathrm{i}})\vek a + (1 + \eta_{\mathrm{i}})\vek b + (1 + \zeta_{\mathrm{i}})\vek c]\) with edges \(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c\), and \(\Phi(\vek\xi) = \vek x_1 + \tfrac12\mat A\,(\vek\xi + \vek 1)\) is a linear map with matrix of derivatives \(\tfrac12\mat A\). Its determinant is \(\det\mat A/8\), and by theorem 4.58 the volume of the parallelepiped is \(|\det\mat A|\).
  3. By theorem 4.59, \(V = \int J\,\mathrm{d}V\). By theorem 4.9 the integral of a polynomial \(\xi^p\eta^q\zeta^r\) is a product of three one-dimensional integrals, and for \(p, q, r \le 2 \le 3\) each is computed exactly by the Gauss rule with two points (lemma 7.25, \(q = 2\) gives exactness up to degree \(3\)).

Source: COOK section 6.5 (PDF pp. 231-232) for the Jacobian matrix. The degree estimate and the proof are not from the source.

Example 15.76 An irregular brick (an irregular brick)

Take a brick with nodes (mm): \((0, 0, 0)\), \((40, 0, 0)\), \((46, 30, 0)\), \((-6, 30, 0)\), \((4, 4, 20)\), \((36, 2, 20)\), \((38, 26, 20)\), \((2, 28, 20)\) (figure 15.39, right). The map \(\Phi\) takes the cube to the brick: corner \(i\) of the cube goes to the node \(\vek x_{\mathrm{i}}\) with the same label. The lower face is a trapezoid, the upper a smaller irregular quadrilateral. The Jacobian determinant has at the corners the values \(3000\), \(3000\), \(3900\), \(3900\), \(1910\), \(1930\), \(2170\), \(2150\) mm³, at the centre \(2700\) mm³, and on a grid of \(21^3\) points the smallest \(1910\) and the largest \(3900\) mm³: it is positive everywhere. The volume by the rule with two points in each coordinate is \(21\,720\) mm³, by the rule with five points in each coordinate also \(21\,720\) mm³, as point 3 of the lemma requires. For the quadrilateral we got the area as \(4J\) at the centre. Here \(8J(0, 0, 0)\) would give \(21\,600\) mm³, \(0{,}55\) % too little: \(J\) is quadratic in \(\zeta\) (SymPy), so its value at the centre is not the average. For a box \(40 \times 30 \times 20\) mm, \(J = 3000\) mm³ everywhere, and indeed \(40\cdot 30\cdot 20/8 = 3000\).

We still have to decide when the map \(\Phi\) is a curved box, that is, when it is injective and has a positive Jacobian determinant in a neighbourhood of the cube (definition 4.65). For the quadrilateral (theorem 15.32) a check at the corners was enough. For the brick, where \(J\) is quadratic, it is not. Let us first see what goes wrong.

Example 15.77 A brick that is fine at the corners and folded inside (opeka, ki je v ogliščih v redu in znotraj prepognjena)

Let a brick have nodes (mm) \((-4, -3, 4)\), \((8, 8, 0)\), \((20, 10, 7)\), \((2, 12, -5)\), \((-19, 8, 20)\), \((31, 8, 13)\), \((16, 25, 13)\), \((-3, 20, 15)\). We found it by a systematic search over random perturbations of a cube of side \(20\) mm (num-10.py), and it is strongly distorted. The Jacobian determinant is positive at all eight corners: \(416{,}625\), \(68{,}875\), \(97{,}75\), \(1040{,}25\), \(1232{,}25\), \(1723{,}375\), \(337{,}75\) and \(433{,}625\) mm³ (exact, SymPy). But on the edge \(2\,3\) (\(\xi = 1\), \(\zeta = -1\)) we have \(J(\eta) = 137{,}34\,\eta^2 + 14{,}44\,\eta - 54{,}03\) mm³, which has zeros at \(\eta = -0{,}682\) and \(\eta = 0{,}577\) and is negative between them, lowest \(-54{,}4\) mm³ at \(\eta = -0{,}053\) (figure 15.40). The axis \(\eta\) leads from one corner to the other, the dashed line would join the two positive values at the corners, as a linear \(J\) would for the quadrilateral. But the curve \(J\) is a quadratic parabola and falls below zero. The map folds on this edge: the brick is fine at the corners, but inside it overlaps itself. We can check this with numbers. The point of the cube \(\xi = 0{,}9\), \(\eta = 0\), \(\zeta = -0{,}9\) with \(J = -29{,}5\) mm³ and the point \(\xi = 0{,}678\), \(\eta = 0{,}373\), \(\zeta = -0{,}977\) with \(J = 55{,}0\) mm³ are mapped to the same point \((13{,}676, 9{,}155, 3{,}796)\) mm (Newton's method, NumPy), so \(\Phi\) is not injective.

A sufficient condition that we can prove is a requirement on the symmetric part of the Jacobian matrix. Its advantage is that it too can be checked on a grid of points and that it does not speak only about the corners.

Lemma 15.78 A sufficient condition for a curved box (zadosten pogoj za ukrivljen kvader)

Let \(\Phi\) be a polynomial map from space to space and \(K = [-1, 1]^3\). If the symmetric part \(\tfrac12(\mat F_\Phi + \mat F_\Phi^\T)\) of the matrix of derivatives is positive definite at every point of the cube \(K\), then there is an open convex set \(D \supset K\) on which \(\Phi\) is injective and \(J_\Phi > 0\). Hence \(\Phi(K)\) is a curved box (definition 4.65), and we may use theorem 4.59.

Proof

We must show that the condition holds on a neighbourhood of the cube, then that \(J_\Phi > 0\) and that \(\Phi\) is injective.

  1. Let \(\mat S(\vek x) = \tfrac12(\mat F_\Phi + \mat F_\Phi^\T)\) at the point \(\vek x\) and let \(m(\vek x)\) be the smallest value of the number \(\vek v\cdot\mat S(\vek x)\vek v\) over unit vectors \(\vek v\). It exists by theorem 1.78, since the unit sphere is closed and bounded, and by the hypothesis \(m(\vek x) > 0\) for \(\vek x \in K\). For a unit \(\vek v\) we have \(|v_{\mathrm{i}}v_{\mathrm{j}}| \le 1\), so in passing from \(\vek x\) to \(\vek x'\) the number \(\vek v\cdot\mat S\vek v\), and with it \(m\), changes at most by the sum \(s(\vek x, \vek x')\) of the absolute values of the changes of the nine entries of \(\mat S\). The entries are polynomials, so \(m\) is continuous and has on \(K\) a smallest value \(m_{\mathrm{K}} > 0\) (theorem 1.78).
  2. The entries of \(\mat S\) are continuous on the closed and bounded set of points at a distance at most \(1\) from \(K\), so they are uniformly continuous there (theorem 4.6). So there is an \(\epsilon \in (0, 1)\) with \(s(\vek x, \vek x') < m_{\mathrm{K}}/2\) whenever \(|\vek x - \vek x'| < \epsilon\). Let \(D\) be the set of points at a distance less than \(\epsilon\) from \(K\). For \(\vek x \in D\) some \(\vek x' \in K\) is closer than \(\epsilon\), so \(m(\vek x) > m(\vek x') - m_{\mathrm{K}}/2 \ge m_{\mathrm{K}}/2 > 0\). The set \(D\) is open. It is convex because \(K\) is convex: if \(\vek x\) and \(\vek y\) are closer than \(\epsilon\) to the points \(\vek x'\) and \(\vek y'\) of \(K\), then \((1 - t)\vek x + t\vek y\) is closer than \(\epsilon\) to the point \((1 - t)\vek x' + t\vek y' \in K\).
  3. Let \(\vek x \in D\) and \(\mat F = \mat F_\Phi(\vek x)\). For \(s \in [0, 1]\) let \(\mat F_{\mathrm{s}} = (1 - s)\mat I + s\mat F\). The symmetric part of \(\mat F_{\mathrm{s}}\) is \((1 - s)\mat I + s\,\mathrm{sym}\,\mat F\), positive definite, so \(\mat F_{\mathrm{s}}\vek v \ne \vek 0\) for \(\vek v \ne \vek 0\) (otherwise \(\vek v\cdot\mat F_{\mathrm{s}}\vek v = 0\)). By lemma 2.53 on the zero determinant, \(\det\mat F_{\mathrm{s}} \ne 0\) for every \(s\). The function \(s \mapsto \det\mat F_{\mathrm{s}}\) is continuous and equals \(1\) at \(s = 0\), so it stays positive up to \(s = 1\): \(J_\Phi(\vek x) > 0\).
  4. Let \(\vek p \ne \vek q\) be in \(D\). The segment between them lies in \(D\), because \(D\) is convex. The function \(s \mapsto \Phi(\vek q + s(\vek p - \vek q))\) has by the chain rule the derivative \(\mat F_\Phi(\ldots)(\vek p - \vek q)\), and by the fundamental theorem of calculus \(\Phi(\vek p) - \Phi(\vek q) = \int_0^1\mat F_\Phi(\vek q + s(\vek p - \vek q))(\vek p - \vek q)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
